line-of-the-mason.description: Neachdan the mason and his descendants, from the first fire to the end of the line.

the-mist.description: Manannan's mist, which hid the island from the ships beyond it, and its thinning.

the-old-ones.description: The people before the Dia-thìrich, their middens, towers, tally-stones and graves, and how the godkin's households met, traded with and outlasted them.

the-seven-coals.description: The seven coals of the vein: their finding, their lighting, their rule and their failing.

events.title: The mason's fire
events.body: Neachdan, a mason splitting rock for a well, breaks into a vein of hard coal that shows every colour in the break. That night a storm comes over the hills, and lightning strikes the broken vein, and it takes fire. He carries a burning coal home and lays the first hearth: it is the first fire of the Dia-thìrich. On it he tries the other coals he broke out, and all burn alike, with a low black flame; he is glad of the fire all the same.

events.title: The spring under the shoulder of the hill fails
events.body: The spring that fed Neachdan's valley thins through a wet season and fails by the dark of the year, leaving four households to carry water a mile and a half by skin. The valley meets and chooses to sink a well of its own.

events.body: The households of the failed spring choose Neachdan, the best splitter of stone among them, to dig a new well. He has already gone to mark the shaft while the others are still weighing whether the old spring might return.

events.title: Neachdan's hands split at the knuckle
events.body: Through the dead of the year Neachdan digs the new well with wedge and oak maul in sleet and frost. His hands split at the knuckle and never close between one day's work and the next, and Sorcha rubs sheep-fat into the cracks each night.

events.title: Neachdan fills his tunic with the coloured stone
events.body: Breaking into the black seam, Neachdan finds pieces streaked gold, white, red-brown and silver, and one that holds every colour at once. Knowing no name or use for them, he judges them too beautiful to leave in the flooding shaft and carries them home against his chest.

events.title: Neachdan shelters as the storm breaks
events.body: A storm comes up the valley at dusk with a green-black sky. Neachdan caps the shaft and takes shelter under a crag above it rather than go back down into a flooding hole, and watches the light change to a thick yellow-brown before the sky breaks.

events.title: Neachdan finds the vein still burning under the rain
events.body: After the lightning strikes his capped shaft, Neachdan uncovers it to find the black seam awake along its whole face, breathing heat and a dark red flame that the driving rain cannot drown, only turn to a thin white smoke off its surface.

events.body: Kneeling at the shaft with his hands held over the burning vein, Neachdan feels warmth reach his split and aching knuckles for the first time since the winter began, and weeps at the well's edge in the storm.

events.title: The household gathers at the first hearth
events.body: Neachdan sets the carried coal on a swept ring of earth in his house. Sorcha, the boy Conall, and three younger children watch the first flame any household on Dia-thìr has ever kept, unsure at first whether it is dangerous.

events.title: The household learns the fire can be fed, and can die
events.body: As the first coal burns down to ash-grey crust, Neachdan breaks it open and finds it still glowing beneath. Sorcha feeds it dry heather from the bedding stack, and the household understands, in one night, that the fire must be fed or it will go out.

events.title: Sorcha burned by the fire
events.body: Feeding the fire a second time, Sorcha brushes her palm against the ash-grey crust of the coal, mistaking it for cold stone, and is burned across the base of her fingers. It is the first hurt any hearth on the island gives.

events.title: The household sets the rule of the stick
events.body: After Sorcha's burn, the household sets a rule kept ever after: the fire is fed with a stick's length between hand and flame, never with a bare palm. Sorcha teaches it to the younger children before dawn, showing them her reddened hand.

events.title: Neachdan says the fire must not go out
events.body: At dawn, with the storm spent and his household warm for the first time any of them can remember, Neachdan kneels by the fire with his hand on the cold earth and says it must not go out. Sorcha pledges to feed it as long as she has hands.

events.body: The household sits awake round the fire through the whole first night, and at grey dawn the children wake reddened by its glow instead of blued by the cold, for the first time in their lives.

events.body: A daughter is born to Neachdan and Sorcha so close to the fire that the women turn her aside for fear of a spark. She is the first child of the hill country to open her eyes by firelight rather than daylight alone. They name her Ailbhe.

events.body: A neighbouring household, its own hearth cold, comes asking for a coal of Teine a' Chlachair. Neachdan gives it freely and will not hear of any debt for it, telling his children that a fire withheld from a cold house is worse than a fire given away unthanked.

events.body: The household hearth drowns in a night of driving rain. The boy Conall runs alone in the dark to the burning vein, scrapes a live coal into a clay water-pot banked round with cold ash, and carries it home to relight the fire. It is learned that fire need not stay where it is born.

events.body: Three days of driven rain come through the thatch in the fifth spring after the lightning and put out the hearth in the black hour before dawn, with Neachdan from home.

events.body: Conall, eleven years old, runs barefoot through the rain to the burning vein with his mother's water-pot, scrapes a live piece into it, and brings the fire home to the dead hearth before his mother wakes.

events.title: The hut on the heather burns
events.body: A near household's fire, laid on packed heather, catches unseen from beneath and breaks into open flame under a heather roof. The family escapes with nothing saved. It is the first house lost to fire since the mason carried his home.

events.title: Conall's word: fire keeps to stone
events.body: Watching the burned household in its ruined yard, the young Conall says plainly what he has half understood since he was eleven: that a fire kept on stone can be trusted, and a fire laid on heather waits only for a moment's neglect to remember what it is.

events.title: Fire reaches the northern moor
events.body: Ailbhe, grown sure of the ground, carries a banked coal a full day's walk north to the edge of the moor at the limit of any household's grazing. Teine a' Chlachair, walked outward hearth by hearth, now burns in dozens of houses that were once each other's strangers.

events.body: Sorcha, who bore Ailbhe by the hearth and was herself the first to be burned by the fire her husband brought home, dies at Tobar dhìreach. The household keeps its fire fed through the mourning without letting it fall.

events.body: Neachdan, An Clachair, dies old by the hearth he lit from the burning vein, having asked once more to be carried to see the well-cut still burning. The household keeps the fire through the mourning as it has kept it every night since the lightning.

events.body: At a gathering of the near hearths in the dark half of the year, Conall sets down standing what he has held since the burned hut: that fire kept from the mason's line should be laid on stone and never on packed heather. The near households take it as their own law.

events.title: Three wells claim the crack
events.body: Tobar dhìreach, Tobar dhubh and Tobar òg each tell that the mason's well was theirs, and that the lightning fell there. Tobar dhìreach can show a capped shaft with a scorched stain on its lip; the other two have only the telling. Between the three no chronicler has ever judged.

events.title: Tadhg's scorched stone
events.body: At the black well two valleys east, Tadhg holds up a dark-faced stone before a gathering and swears the lightning struck his own family's well, not the mason's. The mason's household hears of it and answers nothing, keeping the fire rather than the argument.

events.body: Ailbhe, the fire-bearer, dies in her old age at the hearth she was born beside, having walked Teine a' Chlachair to more hearths than anyone had counted.

events.title: The young well's telling
events.body: An old woman of the young well to the south begins to tell, softly and without a stone to prove it, that her own mother saw the lightning fall into their well and not the mason's. The telling travels further than Tadhg's louder claim and outlasts it.

events.title: Three tellings held at once
events.body: The high valleys settle, without any household deciding it outright, into three tellings of where the lightning fell, held side by side and never set against each other. Only the scorched lip of the mason's own shaft still shows the truth of it, plainly, to anyone who walks to see.

events.body: Conall's son, grown grey at the watch his father left him, will not have the claims of the black well and the young well argued: the fire was walked to a hundred houses that do not care which valley the lightning chose.

events.title: Teine na Fèithe burns low
events.body: Through the years of Muirne's watch the glow in the broken vein fades winter on winter, unmarked by most of the valley, whose hundred hearths no longer need it, and marked only by the one keeper who sits with it in the cold.

events.title: Muirne marks Teine na Fèithe sinking
events.body: Keeping a private reckoning against her own memory, Muirne comes to see what no keeper before her has said aloud: that the glow in the well-cut grows a little lower with every winter, the vein burning down like any fire that is fed by nothing but itself.

events.title: The slab over the burnt vein
events.body: When the fire in the vein has burned itself out, the mason's people dig no further. They lay a flat stone over the broken vein, draw no water beside it, and cut their well again a stone's throw off. In this all the tellings agree.

events.body: In a wet spring of failed crops and standing water, Muirne sits out the last night of Teine na Fèithe in the rain and watches its pale glow go out, quietly, with no one else there to see Teine a' Chlachair die in the ground where it was struck.

events.title: Muirne refuses the digging
events.body: When talk turns to deepening the well-cut in hope of striking fire again, Muirne stands at the mouth of it and forbids the digging, saying the fire came out of the sky on one night only and is not a thing to be dug after in the ground.

events.title: The seed rots in the wet spring
events.body: The spring that finishes Teine na Fèithe is remembered also for rain that stands a hand deep in the low fields and rots the seed in the ground, so that hunger is abroad in the valleys.

told_in.book: Of the Three Wells and the Slab

events.title: Leac na Fèithe laid over the vein
events.body: The household levers a broad flat stone across the mouth of the mason's well-cut and packs its edge with turf, sealing the burnt vein from the weather and forbidding any water to be drawn near it again.

events.title: The new well cut
events.body: A stone's throw from the covered vein, the household cuts a fresh well that gives clean water from its first day, and it is this well, not the mason's old cut, that the household draws from from that day on.

events.title: Muirne tells the covering standing
events.body: Muirne tells the finding and the covering of the vein the same way every year, standing, until her telling is the one the household keeps unaltered: a wonder found, a wonder covered, and a well that gave water all the same.

events.body: Grown too slow for the winter walk, Muirne sends her grandchildren out to Leac na Fèithe to see that the turf at its edge still holds the rain out and that no bucket stands near it.

events.title: Muirne dies
events.body: Muirne dies at Tobar dhìreach in old age and is buried in the ground near the house with no coal or fire laid beside her, having already given the vein's fire, whole, back to the stone. The telling of Leac na Fèithe passes to her grandchildren.

events.title: Conn born to the upper valley
events.body: Conn is born to a herding household high up the Abhainn uaine, further inland and higher than any household of that kin cares to winter, the country from which the summer grazing is followed up onto the shrinking snowfields.

events.body: Grown to a young man, Conn reads the colour of the light on the high tops before dawn to judge whether the beasts want driving down, and is seldom wrong; the older herders of his kin begin letting him choose the summer ground himself.

events.body: Meltwater off the central mountains cuts the bed that Abhainn uaine follows still. On the gravel terraces of its lower reach lie hearth-stones at three heights, each left as the water rose to it.

events.title: Eachna born south of Tobar dhìreach
events.body: Eachna is born to a household some way south of Tobar dhìreach that keeps a fire carried, hearth by hearth, from the mason's own since Ailbhe first walked it outward; she grows up wanting open ground of her own rather than a corner of her father's.

events.body: Hearths are made at Achadh dhìreach, of pine and heather charcoal, with scrapers of grey flint and the split bones of red deer about them. There is no coloured coal in them: those who sat there had none of it, or would not burn it.

events.body: Eachna lays her first fire on a bed of pine and dried heather banked over flat stone, the lesson of stone under every fire carried out from the mason's own household as freely as the fire itself; grey flint and red deer bone gather round it in the seasons after.

events.body: With calves lost to deer grown bold on ground still thin of houses, Eachna's sons take to hunting the moor's deer by torchlight after dark, a burning brand carried low and a spearman behind, working the herds back from the standing crop.

events.title: The oak comes to the lowlands
events.body: The birch and pine of the cold years give way to oak and hazel, as the pollen in the bog under Doire ghlas shows. The grove that names the place stands on ground that was open heath when the vein was first broken.

events.title: The first autumn store of roasted hazel-nuts
events.body: At Achadh dhìreach, under the oak and hazel now grown thick where birch once stood, Eachna's descendants roast whole nuts in the embers and lay by the first store of them against the dark months, rather than gathering only as the season allows.

events.body: Luag is born to a herding household of the northern heath, near enough the changing country of birch and oak that he grows up on the grandmothers' telling of it, and restless in a way his own kin cannot account for.

events.body: Luag of the northern heath follows the grazing past where his kin are used to follow it, until by his twenty-fifth year he has walked ground no one of his household has walked.

events.body: Alone, with a coal carried in a clay pot and dried meat under a hide, Luag walks four days past the last households his own kin know of, out past the last stands of oak and hazel, meaning to see how far the land runs before it meets the sea.

events.title: The bare north-west
events.body: The oak never reaches the north-western horn of the island. The gales off the north-western sea keep it bare, low heather and blanket bog behind the shore without a tree, as it is still. No hearth of that age has been found there.

events.title: The Abhainn ìseal settles into its wide bed
events.body: After generations of shifting across the flat ground below the high valleys, the longest river of the island settles into the wide bed the households along it come to know simply as the river, the shallower side channels running gentler and thick with fish at certain seasons.

events.body: Households along the newly settled river drive the first weirs of hazel stakes across the mouths of the side channels, angled against the current with gaps left for a hand to reach through, and leave the stakes standing once the season's run is done.

events.body: Working alone over the better part of a season, Oisean stretches and stitches greased sealskin over a frame of bent hazel shaped to his own body, and floats it first in a calm inlet, where it holds him and does not sink.

events.body: Alone and with only a paddle and a coil of plaited hide, Oisean crosses the open water to Eilean mhin in an early summer calm and returns before dark with three seals lashed to the frame behind him, the first crossing on the island made of set purpose to a place seen but not walked to.

events.title: Hunters on Eilean mhin
events.body: Seal-hunters pitch camps on Eilean mhin, coming there by boat: the first sure sign that anyone on Dia-thìr crossed open water of set purpose. The camps are kept a season at a time and left.

events.title: The seal-bothies of Eilean mhin first thatched
events.body: Oisean builds a larger boat and begins camping among the seal rocks of Eilean mhin for a stretch of good weather at a time rather than returning each day, raising a shelter of driftwood and hide that comes to be kept and re-thatched, season after season, by those who cross after him.

events.title: Others follow Oisean across
events.body: Oisean's brothers and then young men of the neighbouring households build boats on his pattern and follow him to Eilean mhin, until the crossing in the calm months is a thing the shore simply does.

events.title: The deer of Eilean dhubh grow smaller
events.body: Hunters who cross to Eilean dhubh by boat, the neck no longer drying at all but the lowest ebbs, bring home carcasses lighter than their grandfathers' tellings led them to expect, the island's deer penned by the water onto ground too small to feed a herd that once ranged the length of two islands as one.

events.title: Scàire born to the north shore
events.body: Scàire is born into a household of the north shore that has already taken up the hide boat after the manner spreading up the coast from the south, though built heavier and lower for water that seldom runs calm even at midsummer.

events.title: Oisean dies among boats of his grandsons' making
events.body: Oisean dies at his own hearth on the mainland shore in his old age, by then one boat-builder among many of that coast, his grandsons shaping hulls beside his own with a sureness he never had, having had nothing of his own to look at when he began.

events.title: The weir-stakes renewed in the same holes
events.body: A generation on from the first driving, households of the Abhainn ìseal renew their weirs by driving fresh stakes into the holes the old ones rotted out of, so that a weir kept thirty years stands on almost the same ground it first stood on, though none of its first stakes remain.

events.title: Scàire first goes out to the skerries
events.body: Scàire goes out with her father's crew to the seal skerries off Eilean fhada from her sixteenth year, bailing in boats that ship water with every third swell.

events.title: Seals on the skerries
events.body: Hunters of the north shore go out in skin boats in the autumn gales to the skerries off Eilean fhada, where the grey seals haul out to pup, and take them there. The seal bones in the middens of the north coast bear the same cut-marks as those of Eilean mhin. On Eilean fhada a hard year is counted by the boats the gales kept ashore.

events.title: Scàire sees the grey bank from the skerries
events.body: Master of her own boat and crew, Scàire climbs the highest of the seal skerries off Eilean fhada to judge the weather and sees, lying always along the same stretch of the northern and eastern sea, a grey that no sun burns off and no gale blows away.

events.title: The hard year of the kept boats
events.body: In Scàire's thirty-eighth year the autumn gales hold five boats out of every six ashore the whole season through, the seal harvest thin enough that more than one household of the north shore goes into the winter short of oil for its lamps.

events.title: Scàire master of her own boat
events.body: After her father's death Scàire is master of his boat and crew without much argument from anyone, no one on that coast doubting that she reads a north-shore sea as well as any man alive on it.

events.body: Scàire dies at her own hearth in old age, remembered by her kin less for the grey bank on the northern sea, by then known to every household of that coast, than for a working life spent bringing crews home whole across water that forgave very little.

events.title: The flood-plain of Abhainn ìseal
events.body: Abhainn ìseal, the longest river of the island, settles into the wide bed it keeps now. Fish-weirs of hazel stakes are set across its side channels, and the stakes are renewed in the same holes for generations.

events.title: Children wade the shallows at weir-mending
events.body: Children of the households along the Abhainn ìseal grow up wading the shallows at weir-mending time, knowing which hole takes a stake easily and which fights it long before they know why the holes are where they are.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Weirs on the Abhainn ìseal

events.title: The salmon run first feasted at the weirs
events.body: Households up and down the Abhainn ìseal gather for the first time at the largest of the weirs when the salmon run stands at its thickest, sharing out the catch between more hands than any one household's own rather than guarding it apart.

events.title: The middens of Seann Dunn
events.body: The Seann-Dhaoine begin the great mound at Seann Dunn: limpet shell, seal bone and burnt weed, laid down over many lifetimes until it stands taller than a man. It is the first sure trace of them. No tool in it is shaped as any later Dia-thìreach shaped tools.

events.title: The heap's fire kept through the three-day gale
events.body: A winter gale tears the roof from the shelter behind the shell heap at Dunn and drives the sea over the gathering-rocks for three days; the fire kept at the heap's foot is banked low and fed through the storm by whoever can be spared, and does not go out.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The middens of Seann Dunn

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: I. Of the Heap at Dunn

events.title: The heap worked with the foot
events.body: A woman of Dunn keeps the heap as her mother taught her, letting each bag of shell fall where the heap wants it and working it level with her foot, with the burnt weed laid in thin.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The middens of Seann Dunn

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: I. Of the Heap at Dunn

events.title: The gatherer's mother dies at the tide
events.body: An old woman of the Dunn heap, who has worked the shore pools long past when her hands were fit for it, is found sitting against a rock with the tide turning round her feet, dead as quietly as she lived; what is done with her is not carried past the household's own places.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The middens of Seann Dunn

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: II. Of the Height of a Man

events.title: A season worked alone at the heap
events.body: Through the season after her mother's death the gatherer works the shore pools alone, going down before light and coming up after dark, and keeps the heap's fire no lower than it was kept with two pairs of hands, before her own daughter is old enough to work beside her.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The middens of Seann Dunn

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: II. Of the Height of a Man

events.title: Eggs taken from the low cliffs at Dunn
events.body: The gatherers of Dunn take eggs from the ledges of the low cliffs in the dry months, never so many from one ledge that the birds do not come back to it the next year.

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: I. Of the Heap at Dunn

events.title: An old scraper turned up in the heap
events.body: Loosening an old shoulder of the Dunn heap, a girl finds a flint scraper struck and finished unlike any tool freshly made at the heap's fire that same season; she turns it over a while and lets it fall back into the shell with everything else the heap has taken in.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The middens of Seann Dunn

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: II. Of the Height of a Man

events.title: The heap first used to watch the sea
events.body: A boy sent to fetch fire down for the smoking of fish remarks, standing at the heap's foot, that its top gives the farthest view of the water on that stretch of coast; after that day the heap is climbed from time to time to watch for boats or weather.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The middens of Seann Dunn

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: II. Of the Height of a Man

events.title: The Dunn heap stands a man's height
events.body: The shell heap above the shore at Dunn, built shell by shell and bag by bag over more lifetimes than any one gatherer can reckon, now stands higher at its crown than a grown man can reach with his arm raised, the tallest thing on that shore.

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: II. Of the Height of a Man

events.title: The net-maker of Cwen begins the long mesh
events.body: At Cwen, on the sheltered bay to the south, a net-maker who has always set short nets from each shallow toward an open channel begins, over a winter's close work by the fire, twisting a mesh long enough to close the whole width of the bay's mouth.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The notched net-weights of Seann Chwen

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: III. Of the Net-Maker of Cwen

events.title: The Cwen nets first set across the bay
events.body: The net-maker's household stakes a single unbroken net from shallow to shallow across the mouth of the bay at Cwen for the first time, the net-maker herself wading the deepest channel to sink the centre true; more fish come against it than the smoking-racks can hold.

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: III. Of the Net-Maker of Cwen

events.title: Households come to see the closed net
events.body: Word of the catch taken at the closed net travels the shore, and households from some way off come to see the long line of stakes and weights for themselves, going home to lengthen their own nets by whatever means each knows.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The notched net-weights of Seann Chwen

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: III. Of the Net-Maker of Cwen

events.title: The net-maker's daughter learns the groove
events.body: The net-maker's daughter, grown old enough for close work, begins sitting beside her mother through whole afternoons at the stone weights, learning by eye alone which beach stones will split true under the pecking and which will shatter wrong.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The notched net-weights of Seann Chwen

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: III. Of the Net-Maker of Cwen

events.title: The daughter's first spoiled stones
events.body: Given a stone and the small flint used for the cutting, the net-maker's daughter is set to notching the three strokes; her first attempts run too long, too short or crossing, and each spoiled stone goes back to the unworked pile without comment.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The notched net-weights of Seann Chwen

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: IV. Of the Three Strokes

events.title: The net-maker's eyes fail first
events.body: The net-maker of Cwen gives the finer judging of the stones over to her daughter's sharper sight some while before her own hands fail her.

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: IV. Of the Three Strokes

events.title: The three strokes held a breath longer in the light
events.body: The net-maker's daughter takes up a way of holding each finished weight a breath longer in the light than the work requires, as though the three strokes were worth looking at for their own sake.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The notched net-weights of Seann Chwen

told_in.book: Of the Shell Mound and the Three Strokes
told_in.section: IV. Of the Three Strokes

events.title: The notched net-weights of Seann Chwen
events.body: At Seann Chwen the Seann-Dhaoine sink their nets with beach stones, and every stone is notched with the same three strokes. It is the eldest mark on Dia-thìr made again and again of purpose.

events.title: The daughter cuts the three strokes true
events.body: On a calm morning the net-maker's daughter cuts three strokes into a finished weight and finds nothing in it her trained eye can fault; her mother takes it up, turns it in the same light, and sets down the next stone before her without a word.

events.title: Diarmad is born at Tobar dhìreach
events.body: Diarmad is born the third child and second son of Fionnghuala, into a household that keeps the mason's own unbroken fire and a leather bag of seven coloured pieces the children play with at the hearth.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Diarmad first asks why the pieces are coloured

links.title: Fionnghuala takes Poit an Teine

told_in.book: Of the Boy Who Asked
told_in.section: I. Of the Pot and the Bag

events.title: The aunt keeps Poit an Teine
events.body: Poit an Teine at Tobar dhìreach is kept in Diarmad's childhood by his mother's aunt, called by the household only the aunt, who works wool by the hearth while the children play with the coloured pieces.

told_in.book: Of the Boy Who Asked
told_in.section: I. Of the Pot and the Bag

events.title: Diarmad first asks why the pieces are coloured
events.body: Playing with the leather bag of coloured pieces at the hearth, Diarmad, seven years old, asks the aunt who keeps Poit an Teine why the mason's pieces hold colour and the coal of the hillside does not, and is told only that a boy who wants a better answer may go and ask the sky.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Keeper in the grove

links.label: Same person
links.title: Diarmad is born at Tobar dhìreach

links.label: Same person
links.title: The aunt tells Diarmad to go and ask the sky

told_in.book: Of the Boy Who Asked
told_in.section: I. Of the Pot and the Bag

events.title: The aunt tells Diarmad to go and ask the sky
events.body: Wearied by a seven-year-old's questions, the aunt tells Diarmad that the stones are coloured because the sky made them so on the night of the fire, and that a boy who wants a better answer can go and ask the sky.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Diarmad first asks why the pieces are coloured

told_in.book: Of the Boy Who Asked
told_in.section: II. Of the Question

events.title: Diarmad asks the elders and the fire-bearers
events.body: Diarmad puts his question to the oldest of the line and to the fire-bearers who carry coal to the hearths of the hills, and gathers only shrugs and a fire-bearer's tale that the colour is no more real than a rainbow's, which the pieces' own unfading colour does not bear out.

told_in.book: Of the Boy Who Asked
told_in.section: III. Of the Years of Asking

events.title: Diarmad carries the rainbow piece
events.body: From about his tenth year Diarmad keeps the piece that holds every colour and none carried loose at his belt, and takes to turning it in every light the day offers, once holding it bare in a shower of rain to see whether the wet would draw its colour out; it does not.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Diarmad asks the elders and the fire-bearers

links.title: Diarmad asks it of travellers

told_in.section: III. Of the Years of Asking

events.title: Diarmad asks it of travellers
events.body: He begins putting his question to travellers passing through Tobar dhìreach with no stake in the household's pride, reasoning that a stranger has no cause to fob him off, and gets from most of them a shrug dressed in more words.

links.title: Diarmad carries the rainbow piece

told_in.book: Of the Boy Who Asked
told_in.section: III. Of the Years of Asking

events.title: The rainbow piece held out in the rain
events.body: Diarmad is seen more than once sitting under the eaves in a shower with the rainbow piece held bare to the wet, watching to see whether the rain draws the colour out of it; it lies on top.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Diarmad asks it of travellers

links.label: Same person
links.title: The valley names it Diarmad's question

told_in.book: Of the Boy Who Asked
told_in.section: III. Of the Years of Asking

events.title: The valley names it Diarmad's question
events.body: The asking becomes a settled joke of the high valleys, carried from hearth to hearth by the fire-bearers, half in earnest and half for a laugh, until every household near Tobar dhìreach knows Diarmad's question and no household yet has an answer for it.

links.label: Same person
links.title: The rainbow piece held out in the rain

told_in.book: Of the Boy Who Asked
told_in.section: III. Of the Years of Asking

events.title: Fionnghuala takes Poit an Teine
events.body: On the death of the aunt who had kept it, Fionnghuala becomes keeper of the pot that holds the mason's own ember, the office passing to her at two-and-forty as it had passed through the women of the line before her.

links.title: Diarmad is born at Tobar dhìreach

links.title: Fionnghuala silences the joke at her own hearth

told_in.book: Of the Boy Who Asked
told_in.section: III. Of the Years of Asking

events.title: Fionnghuala silences the joke at her own hearth
events.body: When a cousin by marriage mocks Diarmad's question in front of a full house, Fionnghuala answers that twenty years of one question asked is not the same as a mind that cannot let a matter drop, and the joke is not made again in her hearing.

events.title: A fire-bearer brings a false answer
events.body: A fire-bearer tells Diarmad that colour in a stone is no more real than colour in a rainbow and thins when looked at close; he has looked close a hundred times and the colour has never thinned.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Fionnghuala silences the joke at her own hearth

told_in.section: III. Of the Years of Asking

events.title: Diarmad narrows his question
events.body: Past twenty, Diarmad begins to ask a narrower question than the one he started with: not why the pieces hold colour, but whether there is anyone or anything on the island that might know.

links.title: A fire-bearer brings a false answer

told_in.section: III. Of the Years of Asking

events.title: A fire-bearer brings word of a grove where the wind speaks
events.body: Returning from the longest circuit the household's fire-bearers still walk, a woman of Tobar dhìreach reports, more in passing than in earnest, an old herder's warning of an oak grove on the far northern moor where the wind does not blow as it blows anywhere else.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Herder of the North Moor

events.title: Diarmad presses the fire-bearer for the herder's words
events.body: Diarmad asks the fire-bearer more than once to repeat exactly what the northern herder had said of the grove, until, tired of the asking, she tells him to go and hear it from the herder's own mouth.

told_in.book: Of the Boy Who Asked
told_in.section: IV. Of the Herder of the North Moor

events.title: Diarmad gathers every scrap told of the grove
events.body: Over two years he seeks out travellers from the north and west and sets together their thin, half-agreeing tellings of a grove no bird will nest in and no fire is lit within sight of, the first tale in twenty years of asking that does not simply shrug his question off.

events.title: Fionnghuala gives Diarmad the rainbow piece for the road
events.body: Told her son means to walk north to put his question to the grove itself, Fionnghuala gives him the piece that holds every colour to carry loose in his hand rather than shut in its bag, so that he may have the thing itself before him when he asks.

events.title: Diarmad walks north from Tobar dhìreach
events.body: At seven-and-twenty, Diarmad sets out alone from Tobar dhìreach with a coal banked in a clay pot, a little food and the rainbow piece against his palm, walking three days north and a little west into country his own household has never settled.

events.title: A gale overtakes Diarmad on the open moor
events.body: On the second day of his walk a hard west wind rises over the high moor and does not slacken, and Diarmad pushes on through it regardless, his food too scant to spare for waiting out weather.

events.title: Diarmad reaches the grove's edge in the gale
events.body: On the third afternoon Diarmad comes under the first oaks of the grove he has walked three days to find, and shelters at a fallen trunk with a small fire, listening to a gale in the branches that sounds, to his tired ear, less like wind than like many voices speaking at once.

events.body: After three days walking north-west from Tobar dhìreach, footsore and short of food, Diarmad comes down into the oak grove at Doire ghlas in the last light with a gale already roaring in the crowns of the trees.

events.title: Diarmad builds his fire in the lee of a fallen oak
events.body: In the shelter of a fallen trunk's torn roots, the one spot in the gale-driven grove where a small fire might live, Diarmad builds a fire of oak twigs from an ember he has carried the whole way from Tobar dhìreach in a moss-packed pot.

events.title: The Keeper in the grove
events.body: In the oak grove at Doire ghlas a figure of grey smoke comes to Diarmad of the Mason's line, who has asked why the coal of the vein has colours. It names itself Coimhdeach na Fine, the kin's keeper, and tells him of the making of the world by Caoran, the Young God, and of the gift hidden in the coal. Asked how the colours may be opened, it gives a riddle: the sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit; merge the spirits, and they become almighty. From Diarmad's line the telling of the making goes to every hearth.

events.body: The figure names itself Coimhdeach na Fine, the keeper of the kin, made from the smoke of the first coal an Dia Òg woke, watching the island's people for the one who made them; it tells Diarmad it has watched his line since the mason and bids him ask his question.

events.title: Diarmad asks whether an Dia Òg was angry
events.body: Shamed by the telling of how an Dia-shluagh once found the coloured stones and let them fall back into the heather unknown, Diarmad asks Coimhdeach na Fine whether an Dia Òg was angry at the forgetting; Coimhdeach na Fine answers that he only laughed, for a gift not opened is still given.

events.title: Diarmad tries Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich alone against sky, earth and fire
events.body: Unwilling to leave the grove, Diarmad spends two days trying gual bogha-froise by himself: held up to a gap of open sky, buried in the wet earth by the fallen trunk, and set back into his own small fire alone, with no sea near enough to try and none of the other six coals in hand.

events.body: After two days failing to open Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich alone, Diarmad banks his fire under turf, wraps gual bogha-froise back against his chest, and sets out on the three-day road home, saying the words over to himself so as not to lose them.

events.body: All the first day of the walk home Diarmad says Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich aloud, the strange words and the plain, over and over, the way a man says a name so as not to lose it before he reaches the house.

events.body: Home from Doire ghlas, Diarmad stands at the hearth of Tobar dhìreach and tells the household the bones of what Coimhdeach na Fine gave him: the making of the island from drops of fire, the gift buried and thrown away, and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich of the sky, the earth and the sea.

events.title: The hearth's laughter
events.body: A kinsman of Tadhg's line by marriage laughs Aithris a' Chruthachaidh off as three days' talk with an empty grove, and the household laughs with him, gently, glad to have its world handed back the shape it always was.

events.title: Niamh will not believe it
events.body: Told Aithris a' Chruthachaidh in full, alone, Diarmad's wife Niamh hears him out and says plainly that hunger and cold on an empty moor can put much into a man's head that has no business there, and that she does not believe a word of it.

events.title: Diarmad begins gathering the fathers' names
events.body: Diarmad takes up a second labour beside Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, walking hearth to hearth among the wider kin of the high valleys and the northern moor to ask each house how far back it can say its fathers' names, keeping no name a house cannot answer for.

events.title: Old women give up the fathers' names
events.body: Old women who never troubled themselves over Diarmad's question turn out to have kept four and five fathers' names back, and are glad to give them to someone willing to carry the weight of remembering them.

events.title: The first recital of the Line
events.body: On Oidhche an Dealanaich Diarmad stands at his own hearth and says the fathers' names from Neachdan to himself without a stumble, and Niamh, unbelieving still, stands after him and says Aithris a' Chruthachaidh in full because a house should hear whole what its head carries.

events.body: At the first standing of the Line Niamh stands after her husband and says Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, though she does not yet believe it, holding that a house ought to hear the whole of what its head carries.

events.title: Niamh comes to believe
events.body: In the tenth year after Diarmad's return, Niamh tells their daughter that she has come to believe Aithris a' Chruthachaidh without ever deciding to, the way a path comes to lie worn into a hillside with no single footstep marked as the one that made it.

events.body: Diarmad's mother Fionnghuala dies in her own bed with Poit an Teine within reach of her hand, as she had asked, and Diarmad takes up the keeping of the pot himself alongside the names and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich.

events.title: The dark coals tried in driving rain
events.body: At a standing of the Line the kin lay four dark coals bare on the hillside through a night of hard rain, on the thought that rain is the sky's own water as much as the sea's, and find them in the morning only wet, cold and themselves.

events.title: The coals held up into the gale
events.body: The kin carry the leather bag onto the ridge above Tobar dhìreach on a night of hard wind and hold the coals up bare-handed into it, on the thought that the sky's spirit might answer to its own true weather; the wind passes them by unchanged.

told_in.section: III. Of the Trials That Failed

events.title: All seven burned together in one fire
events.body: Reasoning that Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich's merging might mean the coals themselves rather than their elements, the kin burn all seven together in the hearth-fire and watch them go down black and ordinary together, no brighter for the company.

events.title: Sea-water carried inland for the trial
events.body: A skin of true sea-water is carried the long way from the south shore to Tobar dhìreach and poured over the dark coals in a stone basin, the nearest the inland line can come to the sea itself; it wets them and leaves them cold, as the rain had.

told_in.section: III. Of the Trials That Failed

events.title: Aithris a' Chruthachaidh carried to the northern moor
events.body: A fire-bearer who has heard Aithris a' Chruthachaidh three times at Tobar dhìreach carries it unasked to a hearth on the northern moor, and tells it there in his own words, some pieces lost and others changed in the carrying.

told_in.book: Of the Counting of the Fathers
told_in.section: IV. Of the Telling's Going Out

events.title: Aithris a' Chruthachaidh reaches the eastern hearths
events.body: By the thirtieth year after Diarmad's walk to the grove, traders carry some shape of Aithris a' Chruthachaidh to nearly every hearth of the eastern farms, garbled in a dozen small ways but keeping, in each, the one true thing: that the coal holds a gift no one has yet opened.

told_in.book: Of the Counting of the Fathers
told_in.section: IV. Of the Telling's Going Out

events.title: A garbled riddle comes back from the east
events.body: A trader newly down from the east gives Diarmad a telling of his own riddle in which the sea and the sky have changed places and the earth has dropped out; Diarmad sits a long while after, struck by how far a true thing can travel.

links.title: Diarmad dies sure the answer is near

told_in.section: IV. Of the Telling's Going Out

events.title: Diarmad dies sure the answer is near
events.body: Diarmad dies at his hearth with Poit an Teine near him and the six dark coals and the rainbow at his side, telling Niamh he is sure the answer is nearer than it has ever been, though he cannot say what has brought the nearness home to him.

events.title: Deirbhile fixes Aithris a' Chruthachaidh word for word
events.body: Diarmad's daughter Deirbhile, keeping Aithris a' Chruthachaidh more exactly than her father ever told it, teaches it word for word to her own children and to any of the wider kin who will learn it as strictly as she asks.

events.title: Deirbhile teaches Aithris a' Chruthachaidh a section at a time
events.body: Deirbhile sits each of her children down in turn and makes them say Aithris a' Chruthachaidh back to her a section at a time until they have it as clean as she does, and teaches it so to any of the kin who will sit still for the whole.

events.title: Aithris a' Chruthachaidh said at an eastern hearth
events.body: Three mouths removed from Deirbhile, a woman of an eastern household with no claim on the Line beyond distant kinship says Aithris a' Chruthachaidh standing on the darkest night, and tells a child who asks what Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich means that it is a question for An Clachair's own line to answer.

events.title: The mole at Seann Skell
events.body: A mole of unmortared boulders is laid out into the Abhainn naomh from the bank at Seann Skell, long enough to shelter a dozen boats from the current. Its foot lies under water still at the lowest tides, and every quay wall built there since stands on it.

events.title: The old man begins choosing stones at Skell
events.body: On the first day of the warm month an old man of the river bank at Skell walks the shingle at first light and chooses, by a judgement none of the younger men beside him can name, the boulder that will be rolled and set as the first stone of a mole into the current.

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: I. Of the Mole at Skell

events.title: The trying of Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich is let rest at the mason's hearth
events.body: After coals have been carried to unceasing rain, sunk in sea-water fetched home in skins, and set together seven at once in the hottest fire the line's hands can build, and have come out of every trial the same dull stones, Clann a' Chlachair lets the trying rest, the leather bag closed and kept rather than opened again.

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: III. Of the Recital Kept Idle

events.title: A grandson stands against the current
events.body: A boy of the old man's own kin takes to standing chest-deep at the mole's outer edge on calm summer days, bracing his feet on the last stone set and letting the river push at him without giving ground, watched from the bank by a grandfather who says nothing of it either way.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The mole at Seann Skell

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: I. Of the Mole at Skell

events.title: The mole's first winter
events.body: By the turn of the second year the low ridge of unmortared boulders reaches far enough from the bank at Skell that boats which once beached in the open now lie sheltered in its lee, a dozen at a time on a hard night, and the households along that stretch stop thinking of their landing as open water.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The mole at Seann Skell

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: I. Of the Mole at Skell

events.title: The first slab set on the worst scramble at Bral
events.body: A woman of the grazing household above the western cliffs at Bral works a frost-loosened slab, over most of a season, into a single set step at the foot of the worst stretch of the scramble down to the shingle, wedging it level with smaller stones packed beneath.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The steps of Seann Bhral

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: II. Of the Steps at Bral

events.title: The first stone box raised for the dead of Vell
events.body: A household of the low south-eastern headland rows one of its own dead out to the near island for the first time in a boat built broad enough for the crossing, and raises a box of four slabs and a lid over the body, its face set toward the mainland shore rather than the open sea beyond.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The dead of Seann Vell go to Eilean dhearg

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: IV. Of the Dead of Vell

events.title: The flood the mole holds against
events.body: A flood the old man says he has not seen the like of in all his years on the bank takes one small boat downstream and out of reach, but drives its whole weight against the mole's upstream face without shifting a single stone the old man has set, and the ridge stands scoured clean when the water falls.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The mole at Seann Skell

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: I. Of the Mole at Skell

events.title: Other households ask for the same lee
events.body: After the flood, households that had watched the mole rise from a distance come to the old man and ask to have their own landings brought under its shelter, and he sets them to the rolling and placing exactly as he learned it, so the work outgrows any one household's hands.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The mole at Seann Skell

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: I. Of the Mole at Skell

events.title: The old stone-judge counts the boats coming in
events.body: In his last summers, too stiff to walk the bank at first light, the old man who began the mole at Skell sits above the river of an evening and counts the boats coming in under its lee.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The mole at Seann Skell

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: I. Of the Mole at Skell

events.title: The steps reach the first shelf at Bral
events.body: Cut a slab at a time in whatever season allows it, the steps from the shingle at Bral now run unbroken to a shelf a third of the way up the cliff, wide enough for two to pass, while above it the bare scramble still wants both hands free.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The steps of Seann Bhral

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: II. Of the Steps at Bral

events.title: A boy runs the finished stretch without a hand to the rock
events.body: Sent down for shellfish on a morning the household is short-handed, a boy runs the whole finished stretch of the Bral steps down and up again without once touching the rock, and laughs at the top of it while the women above, none of whom has ever gone that way without a hand out, laugh with him.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The steps of Seann Bhral

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: II. Of the Steps at Bral

events.title: The steps of Seann Bhral
events.body: Two hundred and twelve steps are cut up the cliff at Seann Bhral, from the shingle to the grazing above. Their treads are worn hollow in the middle. How many feet that took, none has reckoned.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The first slab set on the worst scramble at Bral

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The steps reach the first shelf at Bral

links.label: Caused by
links.title: A boy runs the finished stretch without a hand to the rock

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The steps above the shelf go slower

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The treads of Bral wear hollow

events.title: The steps above the shelf go slower
events.body: Above the first shelf at Bral the rock runs harder and gives up fewer slabs, and a worker of the household spends a whole season on a stretch of a dozen feet that yields three steps.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The steps of Seann Bhral

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: II. Of the Steps at Bral

events.title: An old woman rests her hand on the topmost step
events.body: An old woman of Bral sits of an evening on the shelf a third of the way up the cliff and runs her hand along the edge of the topmost step then cut, saying of the rock above only that it will come when it comes.

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: II. Of the Steps at Bral

events.title: The two hundred and twelfth step is cut at Bral
events.body: The steps from the shingle to the grazing above Bral are finished at two hundred and twelve, cut across three generations of hands that never once all worked in the same season, the last stretch of hard rock giving up only three steps for a whole season's work.

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: II. Of the Steps at Bral

events.title: The treads of Bral wear hollow
events.body: The lower steps at Bral, cut soonest and used longest, wear a shallow dish into their middles before the upper steps have worn at all.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The steps of Seann Bhral

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: II. Of the Steps at Bral

events.title: The dead of Seann Vell go to Eilean dhearg
events.body: The Seann-Dhaoine of Seann Vell row their dead out to Eilean dhearg and lay them in stone boxes facing the mainland. Forty boxes are counted there. No grave of theirs of this time is found on the mainland.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The first stone box raised for the dead of Vell

links.label: Leads to
links.title: No grave left open through a night on Eilean dhearg

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A woman rows her mother out, then her daughter

events.title: The recital said to a gathering that came unsent-for
events.body: On the dark-of-the-year night the keeper of An Clachair's hearth stands to say the fathers' names before a gathering that has walked up from the lower valleys of its own will, without any household sending word ahead, and says Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich after as she has said it every year, and closes the bag again unopened.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Keeper in the grove

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: III. Of the Recital Kept Idle

events.title: No grave left open through a night on Eilean dhearg
events.body: The households of Vell will not let a stone box stand open through a night; an unfinished box is covered with brush and stone until the true lid can be rowed across.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The dead of Seann Vell go to Eilean dhearg

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: IV. Of the Dead of Vell

events.title: A woman rows her mother out, then her daughter
events.body: A woman of the same shore rows her own mother's body to the island one autumn and her own daughter's the spring after, and is remembered to have gone to the boat the second time with a face that told the household this crossing was not, for her, a labour like any other.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The dead of Seann Vell go to Eilean dhearg

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: IV. Of the Dead of Vell

events.title: The fortieth box is counted at Vell
events.body: By whatever reckoning that shore keeps among itself, the box set in this season is counted the fortieth to stand on the low ground of the island, its lid laid last and turned, like every lid before it, back toward the water it was rowed across.

told_in.book: Of the Mole and the Steps
told_in.section: IV. Of the Dead of Vell

events.title: The fish-channel of Seann Toll
events.body: At Seann Toll a channel is cut through a shelf of rock into a pool beside the Abhainn uaine, with a slot for a wattle gate. When the river falls the gate is dropped and the pool emptied by hand. The slot is sharp still.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The channel at Toll cut through to the pool

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The slots cut for the wattle gate

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A child learns the channel by her feet

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A boy loses two fingers to the mallet

events.title: The channel at Toll cut through to the pool
events.body: At Toll a household finishes widening a natural crack in a rock shelf into a channel between the still water above and a tide-fed pool below, following the crack's own line rather than cutting fresh through sound stone.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The fish-channel of Seann Toll

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: I. Of the Gate in the Rock

events.title: The careful cutter begins his rows at Tarr
events.body: Along the pale cliffs above Tarr a man of that shore's trade begins cutting rows of signs into the standing rock with a flaked flint chisel and a small stone hammer, each stroke light enough to take the chisel through a shape without lifting it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The script appears at Seann Tarr

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: III. Of the Signs on the Cliff

events.title: The slots cut for the wattle gate
events.body: Deep slots are picked into the rock on either side of the channel's narrowest place at Toll, true from above the river's highest mark to below its lowest, so that a woven gate can be driven home and drawn again season by season.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The fish-channel of Seann Toll

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: I. Of the Gate in the Rock

events.title: The Toll gate first dropped
events.body: The wattle gate is driven home into the slots at Toll for the first time, one man in the channel to guide its foot and two above on the mallet, penning the fish left behind by the ebb in the pool below for the household to take by hand.

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: I. Of the Gate in the Rock

events.title: Shell first carried out onto the sunken reed track
events.body: At the western shore of Loch chrom, after a wet season sinks the worn reed track sooner than most years, broken mussel shell is carried out and trodden into the worst of the sunken ground for the first time, rather than left by the shallows where it was worked.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The shell causeway of Seann Warr

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: II. Of the Road Across the Reeds

events.title: A child learns the channel by her feet
events.body: A child of the Toll household is led by the hand along the smoothed floor of the fish channel at low water until her feet know which stretch stands firm and which gives, without a word for it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The fish-channel of Seann Toll

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: I. Of the Gate in the Rock

events.title: A boy watches an afternoon of the cutting
events.body: A boy sits a whole afternoon at the foot of the Tarr cliff watching the careful cutter's hand, and counts, by a later telling, near two hundred light strokes of the hammer to finish a single sign.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The script appears at Seann Tarr

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: III. Of the Signs on the Cliff

events.title: The carrying of shell becomes yearly work
events.body: What began as one season's answer to a bad sinking becomes, without any one choice remembered for it, a thing the loch household does each year: crushed shell carried out and packed into the worst stretches of the reed crossing on the same errand that gathers the day's mussel.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The shell causeway of Seann Warr

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: II. Of the Road Across the Reeds

events.title: A boy loses two fingers to the mallet
events.body: Misjudging the moment to clear the mallet's swing at the Toll gate, a boy of the household loses two fingers of his left hand; he goes on working the gate in the years after with the hand that remains him.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The fish-channel of Seann Toll

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: I. Of the Gate in the Rock

events.title: The gate dropped three times in a dry summer
events.body: In a summer when the river falls low and stays low the Toll household drops and draws its gate three times before the autumn rains, and reckons the late summer by the droppings rather than by days.

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: I. Of the Gate in the Rock

events.title: Shell crushed before carrying
events.body: The loch household at Warr crushes the mussel shell underfoot on a flat stone kept by the water before carrying it out, having found that crushed shell packs and holds where whole shell slides.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The shell causeway of Seann Warr

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: II. Of the Road Across the Reeds

events.title: The reed-marsh flood
events.body: A hard winter's water works thin the shell already laid on the western marsh crossing at Loch chrom, and the household spends the following spring re-packing the low places before the road can be trusted at a run again.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The shell causeway of Seann Warr

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: II. Of the Road Across the Reeds

events.title: The shell causeway of Seann Warr
events.body: A road of crushed shell is laid across the reed marsh at Seann Warr, on the western shore of Loch chrom, a little over a mile long and raised a forearm above the reeds. It is the eldest made road on the island that may still be walked.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Shell first carried out onto the sunken reed track

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The carrying of shell becomes yearly work

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Shell crushed before carrying

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The reed-marsh flood

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A northern-shore family comes to see the road

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The road left to its builders

events.title: A girl runs the whole shell road at once
events.body: Sent to carry word that the boats are wanted in before dark, a girl of the loch household crosses the whole finished length of the shell road at a run without once testing the ground with a toe, the first so remembered to trust it end to end.

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: II. Of the Road Across the Reeds

events.title: An old row cut over and broken
events.body: Somewhere along the Tarr cliff a first cutting is found deepened and cut across by a later hand, worked with the same patient care as the row it undoes; no one of that shore is remembered ever claiming to know why.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The script appears at Seann Tarr

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: III. Of the Signs on the Cliff

events.title: A northern-shore family comes to see the road
events.body: A household from further round Loch chrom's northern shore walks the finished road from end to end and home again, but goes the long way about on their own crossing rather than tread the loch household's shell a second time.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The shell causeway of Seann Warr

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: II. Of the Road Across the Reeds

events.title: The road left to its builders
events.body: The household that laid the shell road keeps it as a household keeps a hearth, and a stranger's foot on another household's shell is not a thing lightly done on that shore.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The shell causeway of Seann Warr

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: II. Of the Road Across the Reeds

events.title: The script appears at Seann Tarr
events.body: Rows of signs are cut into the cliff above Seann Tarr, in the script that is found afterwards on the standing stones. It is not Dia-thìris, and none has read it. No sign of it has a meaning that all accept.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The careful cutter begins his rows at Tarr

links.label: Caused by
links.title: A boy watches an afternoon of the cutting

links.label: Caused by
links.title: An old row cut over and broken

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The first row cut on the cliff at Tarr

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A woman of Toll walks the coast and finds the cliff

events.title: The first row cut on the cliff at Tarr
events.body: A man of the cliff shore at Tarr finishes a row of signs cut into the standing rock with a flint chisel, each sign some two hundred light blows of the hammer, and begins a second above it.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The script appears at Seann Tarr

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: III. Of the Signs on the Cliff

events.title: More rows cut at Tarr
events.body: By the time the careful cutter's hand has grown unsteady with age, the rows above Tarr run further along the face than any one person standing at its foot can take in with a single turn of the head, and no later hand takes up the cutting with the same close care.

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: III. Of the Signs on the Cliff

events.title: A woman of Toll walks the coast and finds the cliff
events.body: On an errand along the coast a woman of the Toll household comes to the cliff at Tarr and stands a while in the rain watching it darken the newest of the cut rows against the paler stone around them, before going on her way without speaking of it at either household she passes between.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The script appears at Seann Tarr

told_in.book: Of the Road on the Marsh and the Signs on the Cliff
told_in.section: IV. Of the Rain on the New Signs

events.title: Aodh born at Tobar dhìreach
events.body: Aodh is born into Clann a' Chlachair at Tobar dhìreach, into a hearth that has by then said Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich at every recital for near five hundred years without once carrying gual òir to the sea it is said to answer.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: V. Of the Telling at the Hearth

events.title: A traveller names the sea to Aodh
events.body: A trader up from the eastern farms speaks in passing of grey water without a far shore, and Aodh, nine years old, asks him plainly whether he has seen it; it is the first time the boy understands the sea for more than a word said at the recital.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: I. Of the Boy Who Had Not Seen the Sea

events.title: Aodh works the harvest before going
events.body: Asked by Muirgheal to wait until the barley is in and the beasts settled, Aodh works that harvest with more will than any before it, as a man works to leave a thing clean behind him.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Muirgheal bids Aodh take all seven

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: II. Of the Growing of the Question

events.title: Aodh tells Muirgheal he means to walk north
events.body: At twenty Aodh tells Muirgheal, keeper of Poit an Teine at Tobar dhìreach, that he means to carry gual òir to the sea before another generation lets Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich lie; she does not laugh, and asks only that he wait until the harvest is in.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: II. Of the Growing of the Question

events.title: Muirgheal bids Aodh take all seven
events.body: Muirgheal tells Aodh to carry all seven pieces to the sea and not the gold alone, since the seven came out of the mason's tunic together and ought to go together, so that whatever answers answers among its own.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

links.label: Same person
links.title: Aodh works the harvest before going

links.label: Same person
links.title: Aodh sleeps a night above the tideline

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: III. Of the Walk North

events.title: Aodh sets out for the northern shore
events.body: With the harvest under thatch and the beasts driven in from the high pasture, Aodh sets out alone from Tobar dhìreach with all seven coals of the vein wrapped against his chest, walking north across the moor toward a sea he has never seen.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: II. Of the Growing of the Question

events.title: Aodh's first sight of the sea
events.body: Aodh comes over the last rise of the moor and stands before the open sea for the first time in his life, understanding only then, by its slow endless heave, why no telling at any hearth had ever thought the word alone enough to carry it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: III. Of the Walk North

events.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea
events.body: Aodh of the Mason's line carries the seven coals of the vein down to the northern shore, below where Ceann thais now stands, and throws them into the sea one by one. The coal with the sheen of gold takes fire on the water and burns gold until the waves put it under; the other six sink. It is the first of the Seven Coals to be lit from its own spirit.

links.title: New pieces of the vein found in the stream-bank

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Ailean wades after the burning gold

events.title: Gual òir takes fire on the sea
events.body: Aodh throws na Seachd Guail of the vein into the sea one by one from the northern shingle; six sink as any coal sinks, and the coal with the sheen of gold takes fire on the swell and burns gold until a breaker rolls it under.

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: IV. Of the Casting

events.title: Muirgheal weeps at the telling of the gold
events.body: Hearing Aodh's account at the hearth of Tobar dhìreach, old Muirgheal weeps before the gathered kin, near five hundred years since the grove, and says that Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich is proved true: each coal answers to its own element.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: V. Of the Telling at the Hearth

events.title: The name gual òir said at the recital
events.body: For the first time since the mason's own well a new line is added to the recital after the fathers' names, telling of gual òir's lighting on the northern sea; from that night the piece is called gual òir at every telling that carries it on.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: V. Of the Telling at the Hearth

events.title: Word of gual òir spreads from Tobar dhìreach
events.body: Households a half-day's walk and more from Tobar dhìreach send someone to ask whether the telling of gual òir is true, and for days Poit an Teine's door stands open near the whole day to let in one more household wanting to hear it from Aodh's own mouth.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: V. Of the Telling at the Hearth

events.title: Aodh sleeps a night above the tideline
events.body: Aodh does not throw the coals on the evening he reaches the shore, but sleeps in a hollow above the tideline and listens all night to a sound he has never heard before.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Muirgheal bids Aodh take all seven

links.label: Same person
links.title: A new line added to the recital

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: IV. Of the Casting

events.title: A new line added to the recital
events.body: For the first time since the mason a new line is added after the fathers' names at the recital: that gual òir was thrown into the northern sea by Aodh and burned gold until the water put it under.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

links.label: Same person
links.title: Aodh sleeps a night above the tideline

links.label: Same person
links.title: The six held up in a hard frost

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: V. Of the Telling at the Hearth

events.title: Aodh tries the six coals against ground, water and air
events.body: In the years after the gold, Aodh carries the six unanswered coals to hilltop, black peat and standing rainwater within a day's walk of Tobar dhìreach, and once holds one to the bare air in a hard frost, and none of them answers him.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: VI. Of the Six That Would Not Answer

events.title: Muirgheal dies at Tobar dhìreach
events.body: Muirgheal, keeper of Poit an Teine, dies an old woman having lived to hear the sea answer and wept for it; she is carried out and laid as her own mother was before her, the hearth-fire kept burning the whole night through.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: VI. Of the Six That Would Not Answer

events.title: The six held up in a hard frost
events.body: Aodh holds the six dark pieces up on an open palm in a hard frost, as Diarmad was said to have held the rainbow to the sky, and the bare air does not answer.

links.label: Same person
links.title: A new line added to the recital

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: VI. Of the Six That Would Not Answer

events.title: Aodh dies at Tobar dhìreach
events.body: Aodh dies at eight-and-sixty years with the six unanswered coals still kept under his own hand; the recital adds his name after the fathers' names down from Neachdan, and tells that six of the seven still wait to be answered.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: VI. Of the Six That Would Not Answer

events.title: New pieces of the vein found in the stream-bank
events.body: A boy of Aodh's own house, following a strayed goat below Tobar dhìreach, finds the black vein showing bare in a stream-bank cut fresh by a hard season's rain, and the line for the first time since Neachdan holds more coal than the seven old pieces kept in the leather bag.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: VII. Of the New Pieces from the Stream-Bank

events.title: The new pieces passed hand to hand at the recital
events.body: At the recital after the stream-bank finding the fresh pieces of the vein are passed round the gathered kin before the fire is banked, so that every soul there may hold a piece not yet tried against anything.

told_in.book: Of Aodh and the Northern Sea
told_in.section: VII. Of the New Pieces from the Stream-Bank

events.title: The fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn
events.body: Stone-lined pits with short flues are built above the beach at Seann Mhorn, to dry the catch over peat smoke. Seven are known. They are the first buildings on Dia-thìr made for a trade, and not for sleep or for the dead.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The seventh kiln-pit dug at Morn

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The kiln smoke seen from inland

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A kiln is fed with dry peat only

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The fourth pit drowned in a night's rain
