told_in.book: Of the Steersman
told_in.section: I. Of the Word of the West

events.title: Bran begins the great hull
events.body: Bran starts gathering bull-hides cured harder and longer than any boat on his coast has needed, and sets ribs of hazel and ash closer than a hand's width, telling his kin at first only that he means a bigger boat for a bigger catch.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The First Canoe

links.title: The great hull decked with sealed skins

told_in.section: II. Of the Boat He Stitched

events.title: The great hull decked with sealed skins
events.body: Bran decks half the length of his great hull with skins stretched and sealed against green water and sets his ribs closer than three fingers apart, and the neighbours stop believing he builds only for a bigger catch.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Bran begins the great hull

links.label: Same person
links.title: Bran tells his mother the boat's purpose

told_in.book: Of the Steersman
told_in.section: II. Of the Boat He Stitched

events.title: Bran tells his mother the boat's purpose
events.body: Two winters into the building, Bran tells his mother plainly that he means to sail west and prove Aithris a' Chruthachaidh's word of a land beyond the sea's edge true or false. She does not forbid him, though she warns him no telling yet has anyone to bring it home.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The First Canoe

links.title: The great hull decked with sealed skins

links.title: The great hull finished

told_in.book: Of the Steersman
told_in.section: I. Of the Word of the West

events.title: The great hull finished
events.body: By the second spring Bran's boat stands finished on its trestles, broader and higher at the bow than any craft that coast has built, decked with sealed skins to throw off green water, built plainly for open sea rather than the shallows.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The First Canoe

links.title: Blàthnaid's promise asked and given

told_in.section: II. Of the Boat He Stitched

events.title: Blàthnaid's promise asked and given
events.body: The night before the boat puts out, Blàthnaid asks her brother Bran to tell her the truth of whatever he finds, if ever he has the chance. He promises it, a promise she keeps for the rest of her life though he never returns to be asked again.

told_in.section: II. Of the Boat He Stitched

events.title: Bran sails west
events.body: In high summer Bran puts out from the north-west shore with four kinsmen, holding his bow south of the grey bank that never lifts off the northern sea and west into open water no boat of that coast has crossed before. The household sends them off in silence.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The First Canoe

told_in.section: II. Of the Boat He Stitched

events.title: Five put out west, the grey bank on the right hand
events.body: Bran holds his bow west and a little south of the grey bank that lies on the northern sea, standing the whole first morning at the steering-oar and watching the bank fall away astern until it is nothing.

links.title: The First Canoe

events.title: The First Canoe
events.body: Among the coastal Tuathaich families a half-forgotten telling of a voyage is kept, long hushed: a steersman with a name, and a first crossing to an isle of the blessed. Their church tells it as the voyage of Naomh Breandan. The druids of the Old Faith call it idle belief.

events.title: The crewman found on the southern shingle
events.body: A season and more after the boat put out, a woman gathering shellfish finds the youngest of the crew, Bran's sister's son, alive but near dead on a stretch of shingle two days south of his home shore, sun-blackened and too parched to speak.

told_in.section: III. Of the Boy Who Came Back

events.title: The boy's telling of the green land
events.body: Over days of broken whispers the crewman tells of many days on open water, then a green land rising from the sea where fruit hung ready and a spring broke sweet from the rock, and a welcome from a people unmarked by age.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The First Canoe

told_in.section: III. Of the Boy Who Came Back

events.title: Bran stays in the west
events.body: The crewman tells that Bran, offered his freedom to turn home, chose to stay on the green shore, saying he would not turn from the question he had followed his whole life to answer now that his feet stood on it.

links.title: The First Canoe

told_in.section: III. Of the Boy Who Came Back

events.title: The crewman dies
events.body: Eleven days after he is carried in from the shingle, Bran's sister's son dies with the door left open on the sea, saying to the last that the land had not been unkind and his uncle had not looked afraid.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The First Canoe

links.label: Same person
links.title: Bran stays in the west

told_in.book: Of the Steersman
told_in.section: III. Of the Boy Who Came Back

events.title: The telling spreads along the coast
events.body: Within a year of the boy's death the telling of the green land in the west has gone the length of the north-west shore and inland besides, growing surer in each mouth than the dying boy ever claimed it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The First Canoe

told_in.book: Of the Steersman
told_in.section: IV. Of Blàthnaid's Hushing

events.title: Strangers turned from the dying boy's door
events.body: By the fourth day after the crewman is carried in, strangers come to the door asking to see the boy who crossed the western sea, and are turned away for his quiet.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The First Canoe

told_in.book: Of the Steersman
told_in.section: III. Of the Boy Who Came Back

events.title: A boy nearly follows the telling west
events.body: A fifteen-year-old of the shore is found in the dark sitting in a coracle he has no business taking out, looking west, and is brought home and wept over, the telling's first plain harm.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The First Canoe

told_in.book: Of the Steersman
told_in.section: IV. Of Blàthnaid's Hushing

events.title: The elders let the telling fall
events.body: The elders of three shore households agree at a closed fire to starve the telling of the green land rather than forbid it outright, answering no stranger's question of it and teaching it to no child who has not already heard it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The First Canoe

told_in.book: Of the Steersman
told_in.section: IV. Of Blàthnaid's Hushing

events.title: Blàthnaid tells her daughter, once
events.body: An old woman by then, Blàthnaid keeps her promise the only way left to her, telling her grown daughter the whole of the boy's account at a covered hearth, and naming her brother at the end of it: Bran.

events.title: Blàthnaid dies
events.body: Blàthnaid dies an old woman, having told the steersman's telling to no one but her own daughter, who carries it on in the same low voice at the same covered fire.

events.title: Brian digs through frozen ground for a child
events.body: When a child of the black-well household dies of a fever in Brian's twentieth year, he digs through frozen ground for the better part of two days without once cursing it, and sits by the raw earth a while after.

told_in.section: I. Of the Man Who Dug the Graves

events.title: Brian marries Caoimhe
events.body: Brian, grave-digger of the high valleys, marries Caoimhe of a herding household two valleys east, a quick-tongued woman known for setting a whole hearth laughing. Three children born to them die in their first winter, one after another.

told_in.section: I. Of the Man Who Dug the Graves

events.title: Brian takes up the grave-digger's work
events.body: Brian, of Clann a' Chlachair, becomes known through the high valleys as the one who digs the graves of the dead, a trade his father had kept before him. He is a plain, steady man, slow of speech, and the valley comes to trust his hands with its dead.

told_in.section: V. Of the Long Keeping

events.title: Brian thinks of the earth at a graveside
events.body: Waiting at the edge of a fresh grave for the kin to bring the body down, Brian thinks that the dead lie still and the earth takes them, and that if the earth is to take a coal it must go deep and be left.

told_in.section: II. Of What a Plain Man Thought

events.title: Neighbours gather to watch the coals buried
events.body: Word of Brian's digging draws watchers to the graveside through the evening: an old man who had tried the coals himself in his youth, two of Sireadh's grandchildren, a boy sent home twice who comes back a third time. The talk among them does not agree.

events.title: The burial words said over five coals
events.body: Standing in the grave he has dug for five coals, Brian says over them the words said over every grave in the high valleys, asking the ground to hold gently what is given it.

told_in.section: II. Of What a Plain Man Thought

events.title: The black coal warm in the ground
events.body: Brian of the Mason's line buries the five unlit coals deep in the ground beside the slab at Tobar dhìreach. When he digs them up on the next day the black coal, as black as a wet crow, is warm in his hand and smoulders as the air comes to it; the other four are as cold as the clay.

events.title: Brian reasons the earth wants its own time
events.body: Standing at a fresh grave, Brian reasons that as the sea took its coal by wading and the sky by the height of a throw, the earth might take its coal only if left buried deep and undisturbed, as the dead are left. He carries the thought to Sireadh, keeper of the bag.

events.title: Sireadh gives Brian the five dark coals
events.body: Sireadh, eldest keeper of the leather bag since Fionnghuala's day, gives Brian the five coals that have not yet answered, keeping back only her doubt that a grave-digger's guess will fare better than the trials that failed before it.

events.title: The black coal set in Teine a' Chlachair
events.body: Brian carries the warm black coal to the hearth at Tobar dhìreach and sets it among the embers of the fire Clann a' Chlachair holds to have burned unbroken since Oidhche an Dealanaich. It catches and burns on, and is not seen to go dark again.

events.body: Sireadh, the old widow who kept the bag sixty years, says at the graveside that the earth took the coal: the answering came at the rising out of the ground, not the lying in it.

events.title: Brian keeps the black coal in his own pot
events.body: Brian makes a clay pot of his own, fired for the purpose, with a lid of fresh-cut turf, and keeps the black coal burning in it for the rest of his life, feeding it wood and heather and carrying it with him at his work through the high valleys.

events.body: Sireadh dies an old woman, having lived to see the black coal warm in Brian's hand at the graveside by Leac na Fèithe.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Sireadh reads the black coal's answer

told_in.book: Of Brian and the Buried Five
told_in.section: III. Of the Grave Beside the Slab

events.title: Brian teaches the grave-digger's trade
events.body: Grown old, Brian gives over the heaviest digging to younger hands he has taught himself, teaching them above all to line a grave true, so the sides will not fall on what is laid in it; he goes on keeping the black coal at his own hearth.

events.title: Brian dies at three-and-sixty
events.body: Brian, grave-digger of the high valleys and finder of the black coal, dies at three-and-sixty, worn by his years of labour rather than by any illness the valley can name. He is buried beside Leac na Fèithe at Tobar dhìreach, near the ground he first opened for the five coals.

events.title: The black coal burns at Brian's burial
events.body: The pot holding the black coal is set beside Brian's grave, still burning, banked low, through the length of his burial; when the earth is given, Caoimhe lifts the pot herself and carries it home, and keeps the coal burning at her own hearth after.

events.title: The count of the coals said new at the recital
events.body: At the next night of the lightning the reciter of the line adds the black coal to the count: the sea has taken the gold, the sky the white-flecked coal, and now the earth the black, gual dubh, slowly, in the dark. Four coals remain unanswered.

told_in.section: V. Of the Long Keeping

events.title: Caoimhe dies
events.body: Caoimhe, wife of Brian the grave-digger, dies nine years after him, having kept the black coal burning at her own hearth all that while and never remarried; the coal passes from her hands into other keeping, banked and fed as it had been from the first.

links.title: The black coal burns at Brian's burial

told_in.book: Of Brian and the Buried Five
told_in.section: V. Of the Long Keeping

events.title: The stakes found in the tidal mud
events.body: A boy minding his household's mooring finds a straight row of older stakes further out in the tidal mud below the north-western point, one still hung with a scrap of stitched hide. No household owns to having driven them, and who did, or from where, the mud never says.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Stakes in the mud below Ceann mhòr

told_in.book: Of the Stakes in the Mud and the Watcher in the Sea
told_in.section: I. Of the Stakes in the Mud

events.title: Stakes in the mud below Ceann mhòr
events.body: The first sure boats of the north-west coast leave their trace in the tidal mud below Ceann mhòr: a row of mooring stakes and a scrap of stitched hide. Who rowed them, and from where, is not known.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The stakes found in the tidal mud

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The stakes shown to children with a shrug

events.title: The stakes shown to children with a shrug
events.body: The line of old stakes in the mud below the north-western point comes to be called only the stakes, shown to children once by an older cousin with a shrug rather than a story.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Stakes in the mud below Ceann mhòr

told_in.book: Of the Stakes in the Mud and the Watcher in the Sea
told_in.section: I. Of the Stakes in the Mud

events.title: A back rises off the north-western point
events.body: Four men working a mackerel net before dawn see a vast dark back rise smoothly from flat water off the north-west, longer than any whale known to that coast, and sink again without spray or sound. None can afterward agree how long it showed itself, only that it was greater than anything with business in water so shallow.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Sea-Watcher first sighted

told_in.book: Of the Stakes in the Mud and the Watcher in the Sea
told_in.section: II. Of the Watcher

events.title: The Sea-Watcher first sighted
events.body: Old sailors tell of a vast creature dwelling in the waters off the north-western coast. No wreck has ever been brought up to prove them wrong.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: A back rises off the north-western point

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The sighting told at the hearths

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The youngest of the four keeps the telling unaltered

events.title: The sighting told at the hearths
events.body: Within a day the four men's telling has gone the length of the coast, and within its second telling the creature has a name that will not leave it again: Uilebheist na Mara. Not every hearth believes them, but the water off the point is from that year Uilebheist na Mara's water in every mouth, believed or doubted alike.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Sea-Watcher first sighted

told_in.book: Of the Stakes in the Mud and the Watcher in the Sea
told_in.section: II. Of the Watcher

events.title: The youngest of the four keeps the telling unaltered
events.body: The youngest of the four men who saw Uilebheist na Mara rise carries the telling word for word into his old age, adding nothing and taking nothing away, and the coast counts this for more than any argument of the doubters.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Sea-Watcher first sighted

told_in.book: Of the Stakes in the Mud and the Watcher in the Sea
told_in.section: II. Of the Watcher

events.title: Criomthann born to the shore
events.body: Criomthann is born into a household of net-menders and boatmen kin, at some remove, to the household that once sent Bran west over the open sea. He grows up knowing the shape of that older grief by its silences rather than by being told it plainly, and it leaves him wary of open water all his life.

links.title: The First Canoe

links.title: Criomthann pulls a boy from a rip

events.title: Criomthann pulls a boy from a rip
events.body: Criomthann, still a young man, pulls a boy from a rip current with his own hand while three grown men stand arguing on the shingle about the best way to go after him.

links.title: Criomthann born to the shore

told_in.book: Of the Stakes in the Mud and the Watcher in the Sea
told_in.section: III. Of the Beacon

events.title: Two drown in water that shows no storm
events.body: A boat close in below the point goes over in a swell no watcher on shore can account for, and two men drown within sight of their own hearth smoke. The loss is not laid to Uilebheist na Mara, the water being the wrong water, but it teaches Criomthann, newly a father, that the sea gives little warning of the moment it means to take something.

told_in.section: III. Of the Beacon

events.title: Criomthann first climbs the headland with fire
events.body: Sixteen years after the drowning below the point, Criomthann begins carrying driftwood and gorse to the last headland of that coast of an evening, less as a plan reasoned out than as a thing he finds his hands already doing, and lights a fire that will not go dark again in his lifetime.

events.title: The beacon on the Baile chrom headland
events.body: A fire is kept on the headland where Taigh-solais Baile chrom now stands, and its ash lies a man's height deep. The tellings say it was lit to warn boats off the water where the Sea-Watcher was seen, and never to bring them in.

events.title: The warning settles into few words
events.body: Over repeated evenings calling down from the headland to boats working too far into Uilebheist na Mara's water, Criomthann's warning wears smooth into a saying his own children can say back to him in their sleep: Turn back. This water is not for you.

events.title: A peat bank kept for the headland fire
events.body: Criomthann's household keeps aside a bank of peat cut for the headland fire alone, touched for nothing else, so that the fire is never let go dark even in the leanest winter.

events.title: Criomthann's wife dies of a fever
events.body: A fever that takes half the young children of the north-western shore in one bad season takes Criomthann's wife with them, and he keeps the headland fire nine years a widower.

told_in.section: III. Of the Beacon

events.title: Criomthann's strength fails the climb
events.body: Nine years widowed, at three-and-sixty Criomthann can no longer carry wood up the last steep pitch of the headland, and his eldest son takes up the feeding of the fire, so that the flame he lit for no reason he could fully name burns on past the reach of his own life.

events.title: Criomthann dies
events.body: Criomthann dies at four-and-sixty in his own bed, three generations of his kin about him, having outlived every one of the four who first saw Uilebheist na Mara rise. At his own asking he is buried on the lower slope of the headland, within sound of the fire he kept.

events.title: A calm summer fills the nets at Ros ruadh
events.body: A run of flat, windless weather settles over the water off Ros ruadh, the kind of calm fishermen pray for and seldom get, and the settlement's boats work it harder than any season in memory.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Seven boats lost off Ros ruadh

told_in.book: Of the Stakes in the Mud and the Watcher in the Sea
told_in.section: IV. Of the Widows of Ros ruadh

events.title: The first boat fails to come home
events.body: A boat with three men aboard, working water well inside what the settlement calls safe, does not return with the tide. No wreckage of it is ever found on any shingle the length of that coast.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Seven boats lost off Ros ruadh

told_in.book: Of the Stakes in the Mud and the Watcher in the Sea
told_in.section: IV. Of the Widows of Ros ruadh

events.title: The second boat fails eleven days after the first
events.body: A second boat of Ros ruadh, with two men aboard, fails to come home eleven days after the first, from a different stretch of the same calm water, and again no wreckage is found.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Seven boats lost off Ros ruadh

told_in.book: Of the Stakes in the Mud and the Watcher in the Sea
told_in.section: IV. Of the Widows of Ros ruadh

events.title: Seven boats lost from Ros ruadh in one season
events.body: Boat after boat fails to return through a summer of unbroken calm, until seven are lost from Ros ruadh with no storm to blame and no wreck or body ever recovered. Scarcely a hearth in the settlement is left untouched.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Seven boats lost off Ros ruadh

told_in.book: Of the Stakes in the Mud and the Watcher in the Sea
told_in.section: IV. Of the Widows of Ros ruadh

events.title: Seven boats lost off Ros ruadh
events.body: Seven boats are lost from Ros ruadh in one calm season, with no storm to blame. It is the first loss laid at the door of the Sea-Watcher by name; before this it was feared only in general.

events.title: The widows name Uilebheist na Mara
events.body: The widows of Ros ruadh are the first to say plainly, at every hearth that will hear it, that Uilebheist na Mara has taken their seven boats. It is the first loss on that coast laid at Uilebheist na Mara's door by name rather than only feared in its shadow, and the naming holds ever after.

links.label: Answers
links.title: Seven boats lost off Ros ruadh

told_in.section: IV. Of the Widows of Ros ruadh

events.title: Kin from three households feed the beacon together
events.body: In the year after the widows' naming, the headland fire burns harder than in any year since Criomthann first lit it, fed now by hands from three households besides his own grandson's, as though a fire fed by more hands might answer for what seamanship could not.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The beacon on the Baile chrom headland

told_in.book: Of the Stakes in the Mud and the Watcher in the Sea
told_in.section: IV. Of the Widows of Ros ruadh

events.title: The ash on the headland stands a man's height deep
events.body: Fed and banked and fed again by hands born after the worst of the lost season, the beacon's ash has by now been heaped on the same ground for so many lifetimes that it stands a man's own height deep, deep enough that a boy sent to feed it can stand in the hollow of it and be seen from below only from the shoulders up.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The beacon on the Baile chrom headland

told_in.book: Of the Stakes in the Mud and the Watcher in the Sea
told_in.section: IV. Of the Widows of Ros ruadh

events.title: Seven empty places on the shingle
events.body: The shingle at Ros ruadh has by now shifted through enough winters' tides that it no longer holds even the memory of where the seven lost boats once lay drawn up among the rest, and only the headland fire and the widows' naming remain to say the seven ever went out from that shore at all.

links.title: Seven boats lost off Ros ruadh

events.title: The seal hunt moves south
events.body: The hunters of the north-west leave the open water and work the southern side of the headlands, out of the Sea-Watcher's sight. The seal bones thin in the middens of the north-west and grow at Caol mhòr and Cuan bheag.

events.title: The open-water hunt gives way to the strait
events.body: Crew by crew, the boats of the north-west leave the open coast off the last headland for the sheltered water in its lee, keeping the whole of their ground in sight at once. The seal grounds at Ros ruadh and the outer skerries thin as the strait grounds fill.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The seal hunt moves south

told_in.book: Of the Lee of the Headlands and the Writing in the Hills
told_in.section: I. Of the Boats That Kept the Land Close

events.title: An old steersman says the island's hand has drawn back
events.body: An old steersman of the strait says, at a gathering for net-mending, that the sea has not grown smaller, only that the island's hand has drawn back from the part of it a man can no longer trust.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The seal hunt moves south

told_in.book: Of the Lee of the Headlands and the Writing in the Hills
told_in.section: I. Of the Boats That Kept the Land Close

events.title: The middens of Bothan a' Chaolais outgrow the old grounds
events.body: Shell and bone rise faster at Bothan a' Chaolais than they have ever risen, until the bothy folk say a winter's leavings there would wall a house. An old steersman of the strait says plainly what the coast has already done without saying it.

told_in.section: I. Of the Boats That Kept the Land Close

events.title: Eimhir born to a herding household of Doire uaine
events.body: Eimhir is born into a herding family of the high pastures south of Tobar dhìreach, in country the hill folk still call the green grove for the oaks it once bore. She grows to the flock and the ground before she grows to much else.

links.label: Same person
links.title: A ewe strays into a defile of the hills

told_in.book: Of the Lee of the Headlands and the Writing in the Hills
told_in.section: II. Of Eimhir and the High Pastures

events.title: Signs cut in the Doire uaine hills
events.body: Inscriptions are cut on rock faces all across the Doire uaine hills, more than anywhere else on the island, in lines that run for yards. Some lines are cut over and defaced with the same kind of tool that made them.

events.title: A ewe strays into a defile of the hills
events.body: A ewe strays in the night up a narrow defile of the Doire uaine hills where the flock is not taken, and Eimhir follows it before first light into a fold of the hill she does not remember walking.

events.title: Eimhir finds the cut stone
events.body: Following a strayed ewe up an unfamiliar defile before dawn, Eimhir comes on a rock face cut with lines of writing no hand of that country claims, running the height of the stone and further, in a hand unlike any boundary-mark or tally she knows.

told_in.section: III. Of the Cutting on the Stone

events.title: Elders of the hills judge the writing older than living memory
events.body: A small company of the hill country's elders climbs to see the cut stone for itself. One tests it with a flat palm and says nothing; another, walking its length twice, says she knows no hand that claims the writing, and holds that the country will come to know it in its own time.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Word Going Down

events.title: The hills come to a common telling of the writing
events.body: Within two winters, gathered out of dreams two or three swear separately to the same shape and out of half-kept scraps no one can trace to a source, every hearth of that country can tell what the cutting is held to say: a thing that does not breathe, and falls on any fire it sees lit.

links.title: The Hollow Man of Doire uaine

told_in.book: Of the Lee of the Headlands and the Writing in the Hills
told_in.section: IV. Of the Word Going Down

events.title: Dreams of the same shape at several hearths
events.body: Two or three people of the Doire uaine hills swear, without having spoken to one another, that they have dreamed in nearly the same shape of something walking the ridges without breath.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Hollow Man of Doire uaine

told_in.book: Of the Lee of the Headlands and the Writing in the Hills
told_in.section: IV. Of the Word Going Down

events.title: The second cutting is argued over at the hearths
events.body: That parts of the writing were struck across afterward, by what seems the very tool that first cut them, divides the hill country's telling: some hold the writer came back to unwrite a part too dangerous to keep whole; others hold the thing named in the writing did the defacing itself.

told_in.section: V. Of the Cutting-Over

events.title: Children go less often alone to the far pastures
events.body: Without any rule said aloud, fewer households of the Doire uaine hills send a child alone to the farthest grazing after the finding of the writing, and fewer let a night fire burn low and unwatched when the wind comes strange off the high ground.

told_in.book: Of the Lee of the Headlands and the Writing in the Hills
told_in.section: VI. Of the Years Between

events.title: Two herders see the walker on the ridge and live
events.body: Caught by dusk driving beasts home, two herders of the hills see an upright figure walk the crest against the last light, breathing no cloud into the cold air. Neither has a fire lit or a light shown on the path, and both come home to tell it.

told_in.book: Of the Lee of the Headlands and the Writing in the Hills
told_in.section: VI. Of the Years Between

events.title: The defile given a wide berth
events.body: By common unspoken consent the defile where the cut stone stands is given a wide berth, and a strayed sheep is fetched from it only by daylight and never by a child alone.

links.label: Follows from

told_in.section: VI. Of the Years Between

events.title: Eimhir teaches her children the fire and the ridge
events.body: Eimhir teaches her children that the writing is there, that no one reads it, and that a fire built where the ridge can see it is a fire built carelessly, whatever else a person believes.

events.title: The first hearth is dug and roofed at Doire uaine
events.body: A household newly come to the eastern side of the hills digs its cooking fire into a pit and roofs it with a slab, showing no flame above ground. Mocked at first, the family's fire burns unremarked through a hard winter, and two more households follow within the year.

told_in.section: VII. Of the First Covered Hearth

events.title: Eimhir keeps her hearth open against the new custom
events.body: With half the hearths of the hill country dug in or talking of it, Eimhir, old now, tells her daughter she will not hide the fire her family has always kept open to the sky, having touched the writing on the stone herself before any household thought to cover its light.

told_in.section: VIII. Of Eimhir's Own Hearth

events.title: Eimhir dies
events.body: Eimhir dies of no illness the hill country can name, worn out by a long life, and is buried above her family's grazing with a stone set on end and no other marker. Her daughter banks her hearth for the last time and does not build it open again.

told_in.section: IX. Of the Years After

events.title: The covered hearth spreads short of a rule
events.body: Within forty years an open fire on the bare floor grows rare enough in the Doire uaine hills that a child raised to one is asked after it at every gathering, though households on the country's quieter edges still keep the old way, and no rule yet binds the rest.

events.title: Laoghaire begins the first pit-hearth
events.body: On a shoulder of ground below his own house, Laoghaire digs a hearth a man's height into the earth, with a blind angled shaft down to it and a slab dragged over the top, and sleeps beside it the first night to learn whether it holds its heat and shows no light above.

events.body: After the inscriptions the hearths of the Doire uaine hills are dug into pits and roofed with slabs. No open hearth shows in those hills for many lifetimes. The people stay, and hide their light.

events.title: The blind bend in the shaft
events.body: Laoghaire cuts the way down to his pit-hearth as a slanting shaft bent near its foot, so that no glow from below can climb it straight, and leads the smoke out through a crack in the turf ten paces off.

events.title: Laoghaire sleeps the first night in the pit
events.body: Laoghaire sleeps the first night the pit-hearth is whole beside its fire under Leac na Fèithe, listening for anything on the turf above, and comes up at first light with soot on his hands and nothing heard.

told_in.section: I. Of Laoghaire and the Hearth Under the Slab

events.title: Two more households dig the like
events.body: Within the season two households of Laoghaire's own kin dig covered hearths beside their own doors on the pattern he showed them, the first word of the pit under Leac na Fèithe carried hearth to hearth the way any useful thing travelled in those hills.

told_in.section: I. Of Laoghaire and the Hearth Under the Slab

events.title: The line at Tobar dhìreach is asked to cover its fire
events.body: Kin by marriage from the Doire uaine households ask outright at Tobar dhìreach why the household of the mason's own fire alone keeps an open hearth. The keeper of the pot answers that a fire never once let go dark cannot now be hidden without being treated as any lesser fire, and the line's hearth stays open.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hill fires go under the ground

told_in.book: Of the Covered Hearths and the Nine
told_in.section: II. Of the Hearth That Would Not Be Covered

events.title: The line keeps its hearth open
events.body: The man who keeps the pot at Tobar dhìreach answers every neighbour who asks why the line will not cover its fire that Teine a' Chlachair is owed better than to be hidden as a hillside peat-fire hides from its fears.

told_in.book: Of the Covered Hearths and the Nine
told_in.section: II. Of the Hearth That Would Not Be Covered

events.title: The custom spreads through the hills
events.body: Within a handful of years it is the open hearth that wants explaining and the covered one that needs none; households across the Doire uaine hills dig their own, some by Laoghaire's own hand, until no open hearth shows in that country any longer.

told_in.section: I. Of Laoghaire and the Hearth Under the Slab

events.title: A branch at Tobar dhìreach digs a hearth apart
events.body: One branch of Clann a' Chlachair digs itself a covered hearth away from the line's own house, keeping the open fire only for the recital nights. The compromise satisfies no one fully and is quietly let drop again within two generations.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hill fires go under the ground

told_in.section: II. Of the Hearth That Would Not Be Covered

events.title: Laoghaire digs for a widowed sister
events.body: Laoghaire digs three more pit-hearths in his life, one for a widowed sister and two for households that beg it of him, for he alone seems to hold in his head how far the blind bend must run.

events.title: Laoghaire dies
events.body: Laoghaire dies at six-and-sixty in his own house, having outlived two of his own children and dug covered hearths for kin across the hills. He is buried on the shoulder of ground above the pit he dug first, which his sons keep in use for three generations after him.

events.title: The nine at the hill camp
events.body: Nine people die inside a hut at the camp where Muileann chiar was afterwards built, and lie where they fell beside a hearth of fresh ash. No wound is found on any bone. The hut is never opened again, and none is buried from it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The hill camp found silent

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The camp is left for good

events.title: The hill camp found silent
events.body: A shepherd going up to a wintering camp in the south of the massif, seeing no smoke rise from it, finds a hut's door standing open and nine people within lying dead beside a cold hearth, unmarked by wound or struggle. None who come after will go in to bury them.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The nine at the hill camp

told_in.book: Of the Covered Hearths and the Nine
told_in.section: III. Of the Nine

events.title: The camp is left for good
events.body: The hut with the nine dead in it is left standing, its door swinging, until the wattle rots and the roof falls over them. Other households drive their beasts wide of that shoulder of hill from that season on, and none resettles the camp.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The nine at the hill camp

told_in.book: Of the Covered Hearths and the Nine
told_in.section: III. Of the Nine

events.title: A family new to the hills builds an open hearth
events.body: Kin from the eastern farms, new to grazing left unclaimed since the camp was given up, build their first house on the old pattern with the hearth open to the roof-hole, hearing the custom of the covered hearth only as a traveller's tale and keeping their fire open through their first autumn despite their neighbours' warning.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hill fires go under the ground

told_in.book: Of the Covered Hearths and the Nine
told_in.section: IV. Of the Hut That Burned Empty

events.title: The empty house with the fire still burning
events.body: A boy sent at dawn to borrow fire finds the new household's door standing open, the beds thrown back, and every soul of the house gone without blood, struggle or track in the fresh snow. The banked hearth burns on into the empty room exactly as it was left the night before.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hill fires go under the ground

told_in.book: Of the Covered Hearths and the Nine
told_in.section: IV. Of the Hut That Burned Empty

events.title: An old woman warns the newcomers twice
events.body: An old woman of the next valley walks up twice in a summer to tell a family new to the hills that a people does not dig into its own ground for a hundred years over nothing; they thank her and keep their fire open.

told_in.book: Of the Covered Hearths and the Nine
told_in.section: IV. Of the Hut That Burned Empty

events.title: Two herders see the walker on the ridge
events.body: A man and his sister-in-law, out after strayed ewes above the old camp in failing light, see a shape walk the skyline like a man and give off no breath into the cold air. They neither call out nor light a fire near them that evening, and come home unharmed.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Hollow Man of Doire uaine

told_in.book: Of the Covered Hearths and the Nine
told_in.section: V. Of the Walker on the Ridge

events.title: The covered hearth becomes the hills' law
events.body: By the year the two herders come down off the ridge, the pit under Leac na Fèithe is no longer a new thing spreading household by household but simply how a hearth is built in that country; a child born there that year will grow old without ever seeing an open fire under any roof but the one at Tobar dhìreach.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hill fires go under the ground

told_in.book: Of the Covered Hearths and the Nine
told_in.section: V. Of the Walker on the Ridge

events.title: Coille Naomh Muileann chiar set aside
events.body: A forest is held sacred long before any order of the Old Faith claims it. The trees knew it first, the old telling says, and the people after.

events.title: The wood-carriers go the long way round
events.body: Households whose fields run up to Coille Naomh Muileann chiar carry their winter fuel from beyond the far shoulder of open ground, two journeys where one would serve, sooner than put an axe within the wood's bounds.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: No axe in the grove

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: I. Of the Wood That Knew Itself First

events.title: No axe in the grove
events.body: The families at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar carry their fuel a half-day's walk sooner than cut a branch within it. The charcoal in their hearths is of every wood but that one.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The wood-carriers go the long way round

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An uncle grumbles at the wood-carriers' long way round

events.title: An uncle grumbles at the wood-carriers' long way round
events.body: At the end of a hard winter month, one of Sadhbh's uncles says aloud, half in jest, that a tree is a tree wherever it grows and a fire does not ask where its wood was cut. No one answers him, and by the next carrying he goes the long way round with the rest.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: No axe in the grove

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: I. Of the Wood That Knew Itself First

events.title: Sadhbh asks what comes of a man who cuts there
events.body: Sadhbh as a child asks her father what would come of a man who cut in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, and is told that no one has ever found out and that he has no wish to be the first.

links.title: Sadhbh and two others meet the white stag

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: I. Of the Wood That Knew Itself First

events.title: The white stag of the grove
events.body: Three hunters see a white stag at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, and none of them draws. This is the first telling of it. The stag returns in the tellings again and again; in this age it has no god.

events.title: Sadhbh and two others meet the white stag
events.body: At the narrow turn of Gleann nan Damh, a white stag breaks from the treeline of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar rather than the open hill. Sadhbh, her cousin Oscar and a boy new to the drive all have clean sight of it and time to loose, and none of the three draws.

links.title: The white stag of the grove

told_in.section: II. Of the Stag at the Wood's Edge

events.title: The tale of the stag goes hearth to hearth
events.body: The telling of the white stag passes from the nearest hearth outward, gathering colour but losing none of its bones. Some elders say the wood itself put the beast out to be seen; no one that first year gives it a name, god or otherwise.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The white stag of the grove

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: II. Of the Stag at the Wood's Edge

events.title: Hunters begin letting the gully's beasts go rather than risk the wrong one
events.body: Carrying the tale of the stag with them, hunters at the glen let a drive go free more readily whenever it breaks for the treeline, at a real cost in meat foregone, rather than risk striking a beast they should not have struck.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The white stag of the grove

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: II. Of the Stag at the Wood's Edge

events.title: The white stag is seen again
events.body: Twenty-two years after Sadhbh's own meeting, a fresh pair of hunters born after the first seeing find a white stag standing at the same treeline. It is taken for the same beast, or near enough that none troubles to argue the difference, and from this second seeing the tale becomes the whole country's, not one hunter's alone.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The white stag of the grove

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: II. Of the Stag at the Wood's Edge

events.title: Sadhbh dies
events.body: Sadhbh, hunter of the eastern households and one of the three who once let the white stag go unloosed at the glen's turn, dies an old woman, having spent her last years telling the tale at hearths that were not her own and refusing, each time she was asked, to make one cause of the stag's wood and the wood of the stones.

links.title: The white stag of the grove

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: IV. Of Muireall

events.title: Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag left unclaimed
events.body: A second forest, that seems older than the first, is never settled, never felled, and never walked from end to end.

events.title: Three paths end at the same line of stones
events.body: The three paths that run toward the second wood from three quarters are all found, without any household having agreed it, to stop at the same low line of set stones short of the trees.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The paths that stop at a line of stones

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: III. Of the Second Wood

events.title: Children are taught the rule of the stones
events.body: Households near the second wood teach their children early and plainly to go as far as the low line of set stones and no further, and to let go whatever strays past it, for nothing lost beyond the line has ever been recovered.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The paths that stop at a line of stones

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: IV. Of Muireall

events.title: Children told to let a lost thing go past the stones
events.body: Children of the country of the second wood are told early and plainly: go as far as the stones and no further, and whatever crosses the line ahead of you, a ball or a lamb or a hound, let it go.

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: III. Of the Second Wood

events.title: The paths that stop at a line of stones
events.body: Tracks are worn toward Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag from three quarters, and all three end at a low line of set stones some way short of the trees. Beyond the stones the ground is not worn.

links.title: Three paths end at the same line of stones

events.title: Muireall crosses the line of stones
events.body: Left watching for evening deer with other children at the line of set stones before Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the nine-year-old Muireall passes into the trees unseen and uncalled. The eldest child, turned away only a moment, finds her gone with no cry and no mark but a small gap in the undergrowth.

links.title: The paths that stop at a line of stones

links.title: The whole country comes up with torches

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: IV. Of Muireall

events.title: The whole country comes up with torches
events.body: Every household within half a day's walk comes with torches cut and lit before full dark, calling Muireall's name in a chorus that carries over the still evening. They reach the line of stones together and stop there; no torch and no foot crosses it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The paths that stop at a line of stones

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: IV. Of Muireall

events.title: Muireall's mother asks the wood to give the child back
events.body: Held at the stones by her own kin, Muireall's mother asks the wood once, low enough that only those nearest her hear it, to return the child. No answer comes but the ordinary movement of leaves any wood gives back to any question.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The paths that stop at a line of stones

links.title: The whole country comes up with torches

links.label: Same person
links.title: The search narrows and ends at the stones

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: IV. Of Muireall

events.title: The search narrows and ends at the stones
events.body: For three days the country works every fold of ground on the near side of the line and finds no print, no scrap of wool, no trace of Muireall's voice on any wind. On the third day the search stops at the stones, not for want of looking, but because there is nowhere left to look that does not mean crossing a line no one in living memory has ever crossed and returned across.

links.title: The paths that stop at a line of stones

links.title: Muireall's mother asks the wood to give the child back

links.label: Same person
links.title: The hearths say the sìth took the child

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: IV. Of Muireall

events.title: The hearths say the sìth took the child
events.body: With nothing found on the near side of the stones, the hearths give the plainest telling that fits: that the sìth, the people of the hills and mounds who held that country first, took Muireall across the line she crossed, and that no household has yet gone in after anything lost that way and come back the better.

links.title: The paths that stop at a line of stones

told_in.section: III. Of the Second Wood

events.title: Muireall's household sets a stone by its own threshold
events.body: With no body to bury, Muireall's household cuts her name into a stone of their own setting near their own door rather than at the wood, so that whoever asks after it is told of a child lost at a line of stones on a fine summer evening.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The paths that stop at a line of stones

links.label: Same person
links.title: The hearths say the sìth took the child

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: IV. Of Muireall

events.title: A grown hand kept near the children at the stones
events.body: After Muireall is lost no household lets its children watch for deer at that stretch of the line of stones without a grown hand near enough to close on a small arm.

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: IV. Of Muireall

events.title: The rule of the stones becomes unquestioned custom
events.body: A generation on from Muireall's loss, no household near the second wood lets its children watch for deer at the line without a grown hand near enough to hold them back, and children born since grow up knowing the rule before they ever hear the reason for it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The paths that stop at a line of stones

told_in.book: Of the Uncut Woods
told_in.section: IV. Of Muireall

events.title: Cormac born to the keeper's hearth
events.body: Cormac is born the eleventh child and fourth son of the household that keeps the bag of dark coals and the recital at Tobar dhìreach, one child among many and not looked to for the line.

links.title: The keeping falls to Cormac

told_in.section: I. Of Cormac and the Four Dark Coals

events.title: The keeping falls to Cormac
events.body: Cormac's two elder brothers die within one season, one of a fever and one of a fall on the scree above the black well, and the bag of four dark coals and the recital pass to Cormac on his father's death soon after.

told_in.section: I. Of Cormac and the Four Dark Coals

events.title: Cormac's brothers die in one season
events.body: Cormac's two elder brothers die within a season of each other in his fifteenth year, one of a fever and one of a fall on the scree above the black well, and the learning of the recital comes to him.

events.title: Cormac marries Aoibheann
events.body: Cormac takes Aoibheann of a herding household two valleys west, who keeps his hearth and, as they grow old together, his fire-pot and his temper both.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Cormac's brothers die in one season

told_in.section: I. Of Cormac and the Four Dark Coals

events.title: The red-brown coal buried a second time
events.body: Cormac digs a second, deeper hole beside Leac na Fèithe and lays the red-brown coal in it, thinking the earth wants more time than it gave Brian; it lies as cold as before.

told_in.section: I. Of Cormac and the Four Dark Coals

events.title: Gual airgid carried to three rivers
events.body: In one summer Cormac carries gual airgid to three different rivers of the high valleys in turn, in case the Abhainn ghorm alone had been asked; each returns it dark.

told_in.section: I. Of Cormac and the Four Dark Coals

events.title: Cormac thinks the grove may hold a leaving
events.body: Through a wet spring while the lambs are born Cormac turns over the thought that the grove where Coimhdeach na Fine stood may hold some leaving that would answer a coal as the ground at Tobar dhìreach answered Brian.

told_in.section: I. Of Cormac and the Four Dark Coals

events.title: Cormac resolves on the grove
events.body: Turning the failed trials over through a wet spring, Cormac comes to think that the grove where Coimhdeach na Fine once stood may hold in its ground some leaving that would answer a coal, and tells Aoibheann he means to carry the four dark coals north to it.

events.title: The maul turns on the red-brown coal
events.body: On the last morning of his month under the oaks Cormac sets the red-brown coal on a flat stone to break it open, and the maul turns on its hard curved face and comes down across the back of his left hand.

told_in.section: III. Of the Misstrike

events.title: The blood of the misstrike
events.body: Cormac of the Mason's line carries the four unlit coals to the grove at Doire ghlas, where the Keeper first spoke, and sets about breaking them there. His hammer misses and opens the back of his hand, and where the blood falls on the red-brown coal it takes fire. The kindred call it the coal of life.

events.body: Cormac walks north from Tobar dhìreach with the four dark coals in a leather bag, oatcake and dried mutton over his other shoulder, and no company, reaching the oaks of Doire ghlas on the evening of the third day.

told_in.book: Of Cormac of the Misstrike
told_in.section: II. Of the Month Under the Oaks

events.title: A month under the oaks
events.body: Cormac keeps a small fire in the lee of a fallen trunk at Doire ghlas for the better part of a month, laying each dark coal in turn at the foot of every old oak he finds, burying them again, and once speaking to the grove outright; nothing answers him.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Cormac sets out for Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of Cormac of the Misstrike
told_in.section: II. Of the Month Under the Oaks

events.title: The blood of the misstrike
events.body: In a temper at the month's end Cormac sets the red-brown coal on a stone to break it open; the hammer turns on the hard surface and lays open the back of his other hand, and where his blood falls on the coal it catches, burning quietly the colour of firelight through oak while he kneels the better part of a day and forgets to bind the wound.

told_in.section: III. Of the Misstrike

events.title: Cormac breaks camp
events.body: With his hand bound and the coal of life gone quiet again, Cormac leaves Doire ghlas the same afternoon, judging that the grove itself had answered nothing and the finding had come out of his own blood and not the wood.

events.title: Cormac's return
events.body: Four days on the road with his wound slowing him, Cormac comes down into the high valleys at evening; Aoibheann, who has watched the northern track for a week, meets him running in the yard, and hears the whole of it before he will go in to the fire.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Bound Hand

events.title: The byname of the Misstrike
events.body: The valley, which had long since stopped laughing at anything Clann a' Chlachair brought home from the grove, takes to calling Cormac by his scarred hand, Cormac of the Misstrike, and he wears the name and the scar both without complaint.

events.title: Cormac holds up his scarred hand at the recital
events.body: At the next night of the lightning Cormac stands at the hearth with his scarred hand raised for the valley to see and speaks the new line: a fourth coal has answered, quick, out of a man's own blood.

events.title: The fourth coal named at the recital
events.body: At the next telling of the Line on Oidhche an Dealanaich, Cormac holds up his scarred hand before the gathered valley and speaks the new line into the recital: the sea, the sky and the earth had answered, and now a fourth had answered out of a man's own blood, called gual donn-ruadh and, oftener, the coal of life.

events.title: A cousin tries the silver again
events.body: Cormac gives gual airgid over to a younger cousin to carry to the rivers in his stead, and lives to see that trial fail as his own had, and to laugh about it with Aoibheann.

events.title: Children shown the old scar in the firelight
events.body: For some years children of the high valleys are shown the scar on old Cormac's hand in the firelight and told the coal that would not break and the blood that lit it anyway.

events.title: Cormac dies at his own hearth
events.body: Cormac dies in his two-and-seventieth year at Tobar dhìreach, Poit an Teine burning near him as it burned near every keeper before him, his last clear word a complaint of the old scar aching in the damp.

events.title: The bag passes on unnamed
events.body: The leather bag with gual airgid, the coal that has never yet been tried by fire, and gual bogha-froise passes from Cormac's grave to a younger kinsman of the line, whose name the recital keeps but does not give to strangers.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Bound Hand

events.title: Aoibheann's last years
events.body: Aoibheann outlives Cormac by six years at Tobar dhìreach, and it is from her telling, repeated at the hearth, that the valley's children learn the story of the coal that would not break and the blood that lit it anyway.

events.title: The deer-drives of the eastern forest
events.body: Lines of stakes and brush are set to drive the red deer of the eastern woods into a gully near Doire fhionn, where they are killed with spears. The antlers of the greatest stags are stacked apart from the rest.

events.title: Dubhghall drives the gully alone for the first time
events.body: At twenty-five, Dubhghall stands for the first time at the head of the deer-drive he has watched his uncle lead since boyhood, and takes a stag with a bad throw that his uncle and two others must finish for him, a failure the household forgets within the season.

told_in.section: I. Of the Glen of the Stags

events.title: The stand of antlers grows at the gully's mouth
events.body: Two autumns running, a good drive leaves the stacked antlers at the mouth of the glen tall enough for a boy to stand in their shadow at noon, the household's plain mark of what the year's meat has cost the herd.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The deer-drives of the eastern forest

told_in.book: Of the Dogs, the Geese and the Farthest Reach
told_in.section: I. Of the Glen of the Stags

events.title: Dubhghall's throw goes wide
events.body: In his first year at the gully's throat Dubhghall's throw strikes a young stag in the shoulder rather than the throat, and it takes his uncle and two others to finish it; he practises the throw all winter against a bundle of brush.

told_in.section: I. Of the Glen of the Stags

events.title: Dubhghall takes the head of the drive
events.body: When his uncle's knees will no longer hold him through a whole autumn morning, Dubhghall takes the head of the line at the gully, exacting in one thing only: that no young man stand carelessly.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Dubhghall's throw goes wide

links.title: Dubhghall's uncle dies

told_in.book: Of the Dogs, the Geese and the Farthest Reach
told_in.section: I. Of the Glen of the Stags

events.title: Dubhghall's uncle dies
events.body: Worn thin by winters and no longer able to stand a whole autumn morning at the gully, Dubhghall's uncle dies and is buried within sight of the glen's mouth, close enough that his grandchildren can point to the rise from the stand of horn.

told_in.section: I. Of the Glen of the Stags

events.title: Dubhghall's grandson's dog dies
events.body: A dog that has slept across the boy's feet every night since it was weaned lies down by the hearth one evening and does not rise the next morning, found stiff and cold before the household is properly awake.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first dog graves

told_in.book: Of the Dogs, the Geese and the Farthest Reach
told_in.section: II. Of the Dog at Cnoc fhionn

events.title: The boy digs the dog a grave and sets a shell at its head
events.body: On the dry rise above the house, the boy digs a grave the length of a dog, lays it on its side as a sleeping dog lies, and sets at its head a sea-shell kept idle on a hearth-shelf for years, telling no one beforehand and asking no leave.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first dog graves

told_in.book: Of the Dogs, the Geese and the Farthest Reach
told_in.section: II. Of the Dog at Cnoc fhionn

events.title: An old woman questions the dog's grave
events.body: At a gathering of the near hearths an older woman asks the boy, not unkindly, whether he means to give every lost lamb a shell as well; he answers only that the dog slept at his feet for nine years and a lamb never did, and she allows it is answer enough.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first dog graves

told_in.book: Of the Dogs, the Geese and the Farthest Reach
told_in.section: II. Of the Dog at Cnoc fhionn

events.title: Dubhghall's grandson asks why no one hunts the geese
events.body: Watching the grey line come in over the water one still evening, the boy asks his grandfather why no household takes the geese of Eilean ghorm for meat; Dubhghall answers only that a people who stop leaving what they have always left are no longer quite the people they were.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The geese of Eilean ghorm

links.title: Dubhghall's uncle dies

events.title: Two more households bury dogs at Cnoc fhionn
events.body: Within a few years of the first grave, two neighbouring households bury their own dogs the same way, a shell at the head and a proper grave dug, and the custom begins to travel hearth to hearth through the hill country.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first dog graves

told_in.section: II. Of the Dog at Cnoc fhionn

events.title: Dubhghall dies at Cnoc fhionn
events.body: Dubhghall dies in his sixty-fifth year among his daughter's family, remembered at his own leaving for thirty autumns of driving the glen without losing a man to horn or wet ground; his grandson sets the last of his kept shells at the old man's head.

events.title: A shell set at Dubhghall's head
events.body: Dubhghall's grandson sets a shell at his grandfather's head at his burying, the last of a small store kept since the dog's grave, saying the old man deserved no less than a dog.

events.title: The young man of the northern moor builds a boat for Eilean ghorm
events.body: In a season of want, a young man of the northern moor spends a hard winter building a hide boat in secret and puts out alone one grey morning for the geese's island, telling no one what the boat is for.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The geese of Eilean ghorm

told_in.book: Of the Dogs, the Geese and the Farthest Reach
told_in.section: III. Of the Geese of Eilean ghorm

events.title: The first dog graves
events.body: At Cnoc fhionn in the east dogs are buried beside people, each with a shell at its head. No beast was given a grave on Dia-thìr before.

events.title: The young man does not come back a hunter
events.body: The fate of the young man who sailed for Eilean ghorm is told three ways at three hearths and agreed by none of them; he is remembered not as one who found good hunting, but as a warning the country keeps without understanding it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The geese of Eilean ghorm

told_in.book: Of the Dogs, the Geese and the Farthest Reach
told_in.section: III. Of the Geese of Eilean ghorm

events.title: The geese of Eilean ghorm
events.body: The grey geese that winter on Eilean ghorm come into the tellings for the first time. They come in with the first storm and leave with the last, and none hunts them there.

links.label: Caused by

links.title: The geese read for the turn of the winter

events.title: The geese read for the turn of the winter
events.body: Households that watch the grey geese of Eilean ghorm close enough learn to read the turn of the winter in their leaving, which comes a day or two ahead of the year's last storm.

links.title: The geese of Eilean ghorm

told_in.section: III. Of the Geese of Eilean ghorm

events.title: The mole at Skell stands nine hundred years
events.body: Mended and lengthened season on season since the old stone-judge first set it, the mole at Skell runs further out into the Abhainn naomh than any one lifetime could have carried it, and a woman of the landing walks its length each evening to look for any stone the current has worked loose.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The widest reach of the Seann-Dhaoine

told_in.book: Of the Dogs, the Geese and the Farthest Reach
told_in.section: IV. Of Skell at Its Height

events.title: A woman walks the mole at Skell each evening
events.body: A woman of Skell who keeps the mole's stones walks its length each evening at the turn of the tide, looking for any stone the current has worked loose.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The widest reach of the Seann-Dhaoine

told_in.book: Of the Dogs, the Geese and the Farthest Reach
told_in.section: IV. Of Skell at Its Height

events.title: Every mooring taken at Skell
events.body: At Skell on the Abhainn naomh, the greatest landing of the people of the shore, every mooring behind the mole is taken one autumn, hulls lying three and four deep along its sheltered face, and the smoke of the landing's hearths hangs over the river's mouth from dawn to dark.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The widest reach of the Seann-Dhaoine

told_in.book: Of the Dogs, the Geese and the Farthest Reach
told_in.section: IV. Of Skell at Its Height

events.title: The widest reach of the Seann-Dhaoine
events.body: At their height the Seann-Dhaoine hold every coast of the island: the ten places whose names begin with Seann, and the islands off them. Their greatest landing is at Seann Skell, up the Abhainn naomh, where the mole already stands.

events.title: The warm springs used
events.body: Stone basins are set into the springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh. The people buried near them have old breaks that knitted clean. Here the sick of Dia-thìr are first brought for healing.

links.label: Same place
links.title: A leg set under the warm water

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The keeper of the basins judges a wound by its smell

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The young keeper takes up the turning

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A child's broken skull mended by the first basin

events.title: A leg set under the warm water
events.body: At Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh the keeper of the basins sets a leg broken through the skin under the warm water of the third basin, binds it tight with wet bark and cord, and turns the man twice a day for a season; he walks out on a stick before the winter turns.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The warm springs used

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: I. Of the Springs Under the Mountain

events.title: The keeper of the basins judges a wound by its smell
events.body: The keeper of the warm basins tells by the colour of a wound, and its smell when the dressing comes off, whether it wants the second basin or the third or neither, and has no words for the telling.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The warm springs used

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: I. Of the Springs Under the Mountain

events.title: The youth of the south-east asks to go down
events.body: A youth not yet grown to his height asks to be the one let down into the eastern shaft at Toll-dubh, and two women of the south-east plait a rope for it from the hides of three oxen.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The shaft of Toll-dubh in the south-east

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: III. Of the Youth Sent Down

events.title: The lamp goes small in the eastern shaft
events.body: The youth is let down into the eastern shaft on the plaited rope with a lamp of fat in a hollowed stone; the lamp goes small and the dark closes over it, the rope runs out to its last knot and hangs, and after a long while it jerks twice and is hauled up slowly.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The shaft of Toll-dubh in the south-east

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: III. Of the Youth Sent Down

events.title: The youth comes up ash-faced and silent
events.body: The youth comes over the lip with his lamp out and his face the colour of ash, and never says, then or in all the years he lives, what was at the bottom; after him no one goes down again.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The shaft of Toll-dubh in the south-east

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: III. Of the Youth Sent Down

events.title: The young keeper takes up the turning
events.body: The old keeper of the basins dies and is buried on the slope nearest the water; a young woman who came up as a girl with a father whose ribs were stove in takes up the setting and the turning the next morning, and sets three bones that day.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The warm springs used

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: I. Of the Springs Under the Mountain

events.title: A child's broken skull mended by the first basin
events.body: A child fallen from a kiln wall is carried two days to the springs by its mother with the bone above its ear broken; the young keeper lays it by the steam of the first basin, washes the break and binds it loosely, and on the fourth morning it wakes and asks for food.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The warm springs used

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: II. Of the Young Keeper and the Child's Skull

events.title: Heated stones laid in the third basin in a dry summer
events.body: In a dry summer when the water runs low from the three mouths, the keepers of the basins lay stones heated in a fire into the third basin to bring it back to the warmth the sick need.

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: II. Of the Young Keeper and the Child's Skull

events.title: The gate of the outpost walled up
events.body: The single gate of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire is blocked with rubble from within. Those who did it left by another way, or did not leave.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The last stone set by lamplight

events.title: The last stone set by lamplight
events.body: One man, left alone at Làrach an Dùin-fhaire's gate at dusk after the others have gone to other work within the walls, fits the last stones into the gap by a lamp burning down, and presses the last one home with the flat of his hand. Where he went after is not told.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The gate of the outpost walled up

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: IV. Of the Last Stone Set

events.title: The rope of the shaft cut up for mooring lines
events.body: After the youth comes up silent, the plaited rope is cut up for mooring lines, and the grown people of the south-east walk wider of the shaft's lip than before.

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: III. Of the Youth Sent Down

events.title: The youth will not let a lamp burn low
events.body: The youth who went down the eastern shaft, grown and married at a landing two days south, is known for nothing strange except that he rises in the night to trim or put out any lamp burning low.

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: III. Of the Youth Sent Down

events.title: Làrach an Dùin-fhaire abandoned
events.body: The outpost is deserted. It lay in ruin before the first trusty chronicles, and it is older than any dwelling of the Dia-thìrich. Who built it none knows.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The kerbed way greens over

events.title: The kerbed way greens over
events.body: With no one going down off the spur, the grass creeps in over the slabs of the kerbed way from its edges, and the kerbs show through the turf like the bones of a thing half buried.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Làrach an Dùin-fhaire abandoned

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: V. Of the Empty Places

events.title: A woman finds the cistern choked
events.body: A woman of the three rings, going at first light to draw water for her sick father, finds the cistern full of whole cattle, unbutchered, their backs and bent legs breaking the dark water; no one of the rings can say who did it, and no one draws from it again.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The fortress cistern fouled

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: V. Of the Empty Places

events.title: The fortress cistern fouled
events.body: The cistern of Làrach an Dùin is choked with the bones of cattle, thrown in whole. Its water had served four hundred people. No one draws from it again.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: A woman finds the cistern choked

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Water carried up the height every morning

events.title: Water carried up the height every morning
events.body: With the cistern of the three rings fouled, every household on the height carries its water up from the valley springs on its own back, a whole morning's labour every morning.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The fortress cistern fouled

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: V. Of the Empty Places

events.title: The first households go down from the rings
events.body: Some households of the three rings tire of the water-carrying before they tire of the height, and go down the track to the lower valleys, saying they go only for the winter.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Làrach an Dùin abandoned

told_in.book: Of the Warm Springs and the Walled Gate
told_in.section: V. Of the Empty Places

events.title: Fewer fires burn along Làrach an Dùin wall
events.body: Through a hard winter the coast-people left within the three rings let the farthest fires along the middle wall go dark first, feeding what fuel is left toward those nearest the gate, so that the chain of lights along the rampart burns shorter and thicker each week that passes.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Làrach an Dùin abandoned

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: I. Of the Last Fire in the Rings

events.title: The last fire in the rings is let go down
events.body: The last of the coast-people still keeping Làrach an Dùin finds every other fire along the wall dark one morning, tends her own alone three days more, then spreads its embers thin across the stone and walks out through the gate and down toward the valleys, carrying nothing from the place she had not carried into it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Làrach an Dùin abandoned

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: I. Of the Last Fire in the Rings

events.title: Làrach an Dùin abandoned
events.body: The fortress is deserted in like manner, and is as much a riddle as the outpost. Whether both had the same builders has never been settled.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The first households go down from the rings

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Fewer fires burn along Làrach an Dùin wall

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The last fire in the rings is let go down

links.label: Leads to

links.label: Legacy of

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The southern middens grow faster than living memory

events.title: Grass in the threshold of the rings
events.body: Within a few winters of the last fire along the middle wall, grass finds a footing in the gate threshold of the three rings, where the feet of four hundred once kept the stone bare.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Làrach an Dùin abandoned

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: I. Of the Last Fire in the Rings

events.title: A grandfather of the western landing will not speak of the height
events.body: An old man long settled among shore kin who never went up answers his grandson's question about Làrach an Dùin only with the cold and the wind that found a man through doubled wool, and will say nothing of why he left it or whether he meant, at the time, to come back.

links.title: Làrach an Dùin abandoned

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: II. Of the Ones Who Went Down

events.title: A household from the rings comes down to Morn
events.body: A household of five comes down from the three rings to the kilns at Morn with nothing but what it can carry, its one ox lost on the scree; the landing takes it in, and the women are set to the kilns, where the younger learns in one morning that a kiln fire must smoke and not flame.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: Làrach an Dùin abandoned

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: III. Of a Household Come Down to the Kilns

events.title: The southern middens grow faster than living memory
events.body: As more of the coast-people settle at the shore than the shore has ever held, the middens of the southern landing thicken season on season with the ordinary leavings of a people's swelling numbers, and a landing once counted by the dozen comes to be counted by the score.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Làrach an Dùin abandoned

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: II. Of the Ones Who Went Down

events.title: The son's wife learns a kiln must not flame
events.body: The keeper of the middle kiln at Morn leads a woman new down from the heights by the wrist to a smouldering kiln and holds her hand over its rack until she understands what three tellings in words had not taught her.

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: III. Of a Household Come Down to the Kilns

events.title: A girl from the heights sees the sea
events.body: A girl of eight born within the innermost ring is lifted onto a rock above Morn by her grandfather and turned to face the sea, and asks, after a long look, whether it ever stops moving.

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: III. Of a Household Come Down to the Kilns

events.title: A worked stone kept on a shore shelf
events.body: An old man come down from a height keeps on a shelf at the shore a worked stone no one there has a use for, and it is laid in the stone box with him when his time comes.

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: II. Of the Ones Who Went Down

events.title: Three men climb to the temple with prising-bars
events.body: Three men of the last kin that still tends the temple climb its steps on a grey autumn morning with bars of seasoned oak shod with bone, the eldest of them a man past sixty who has climbed on the shortest morning every year of his life.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The temple altar stripped

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: IV. Of the Prising of the Altar

events.title: The altar's top stone is prised free
events.body: Working the better part of the morning, two of the three break out the old clay from the sockets with the points of their bars while the eldest stands with his hands flat on the stone, and a while past noon they lift it whole from the sockets it has held since before anyone could remember.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The temple altar stripped

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: IV. Of the Prising of the Altar

events.title: The temple altar stripped
events.body: The top stone of the altar at Làrach an Teampaill is prised off and carried away; the sockets that held it are sharp still. It has never been found, and what was cut on it, if anything, is not known.
