events.title: The altar stone is carried west out of sight
events.body: Slung between the three in a net of hide rope on the same bars, the altar stone is carried down the platform steps and over the shoulder of the hill to the west; it is never found.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The temple altar stripped

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: IV. Of the Prising of the Altar

events.title: The temple platform goes untended
events.body: No one of that kin climbs the temple steps on the shortest morning again; grass comes in between the platform's fitted stones, and the easy last step that every child of the valley once found with a bare foot in the dark is lost under turf.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The temple altar stripped

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: V. Of the Cairn on the Steps

events.title: A cairn built below the empty sockets
events.body: The eldest of the three who prised the altar goes up alone years after and spends most of a day building a small cairn of loose stone below the empty sockets, capped square, and comes down with his hands scraped raw, and does not say what it is for.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The temple altar stripped

told_in.book: Of the Empty Rings and the Stripped Altar
told_in.section: V. Of the Cairn on the Steps

events.title: The easy last step lost under turf
events.body: The last step of the temple platform, flush with the moor, which every child of the valley once found with a bare foot in the dark, is lost under turf, and the climb begins now with a stumble.

events.title: Eòghann born to the keeper's hearth
events.body: Eòghann is born the second child of the household that keeps the bag and Poit an Teine at Tobar dhìreach, not first looked to for the keeping while his elder sister lives.

events.title: Eòghann counts the coals into his palm as a child
events.body: Eòghann, free of the keeping as a younger son, counts the three coals into his own small palm long before anyone asks it of him, turning them over for the plain pleasure of a smooth thing in the hand.

events.title: The keeping falls to Eòghann
events.body: Eòghann's sister dies of a fever in her nineteenth year, and the bag of three dark coals and the recital pass to Eòghann on his father's death soon after; he is twenty.

events.title: Eòghann's sister dies and his father is buried
events.body: Eòghann's elder sister dies of a fever in her nineteenth year, and his father is buried beside Leac na Fèithe the same season, so that the keeping comes to Eòghann at twenty.

events.body: Eòghann takes Dearbhail of the lake-shore line, who keeps his fire-pot and his hearth through the long absences his walking keeps him to.

events.title: Gual airgid carried to the home river and two more
events.body: In his first years of keeping Eòghann carries gual airgid to the Abhainn ghorm below Tobar dhìreach, to two rivers besides, and to a mountain tarn, in case the water nearest the hearth had never been fairly asked; none answers him.

events.title: A mountain tarn tried for the silver
events.body: Among the waters Eòghann tries gual airgid against is a mountain tarn that is no river at all but holds, by the telling, water enough to be worth the asking; it does not answer.

events.title: Eòghann keeps the old custom of the shore
events.body: With nothing newly occurring to him, Eòghann carries the three dark coals north to the shore his father once brought him to, to throw them into the sea in the old way, out of a custom kept past most keepers' belief in it.

events.body: Eòghann throws the silver, the untried, and gual bogha-froise into the grey swell off the northern shore in the falling light, and wades in after them to find them as dark and salt-wet as they went in.

events.title: Eòghann walks home through two days of rain
events.body: Eòghann turns south for Tobar dhìreach the morning after the casting, walking two wet days over moor and birch scrub with his mind on nothing beyond the ground in front of him.

told_in.section: II. Of the Northern Shore

events.title: The silver coal in the river
events.body: Eòghann of the Mason's line drinks from the Abhainn ghorm below Tobar dhìreach and says, 'This water tastes different from the sea water.' He throws the three unlit coals into the stream, and the coal with the sheen of silver takes fire in the current and burns silver under the water. The coal of fire and the rainbow coal lie dark.

events.body: Thirsty and tired on the last stretch of the road home, Eòghann kneels at the crossing of the Abhainn ghorm below Tobar dhìreach and drinks, and says aloud, to no one, that this water tastes different from the sea water.

events.body: Gual teine and the rainbow, rolled on past Eòghann by the current in the dark, are found at first light lodged cold against a bar of gravel a stone's throw below the crossing, and carried home in the bag as dark as they went into the water.

events.title: The fifth coal named at the recital
events.body: At the next telling of the Line, Eòghann speaks the new line into the recital: the sea, the height, the earth and a man's own blood have answered, and now the river has taken the fifth, given rather than thrown to it, and the valley names it gual airgid.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Recital

events.title: The silver burns on under the crossing
events.body: Gual airgid goes on burning under the current at the shallow crossing below Tobar dhìreach, a low pale light any traveller may kneel at the bank and see on a dark evening.

told_in.section: III. Of the Abhainn Ghorm

events.title: Travellers come to see the fire under the water
events.body: Word of the pale fire standing under the current draws travellers to the crossing below Tobar dhìreach in numbers greater than the ford had ever seen, some kneeling to drink the same water Eòghann drank without finding it tastes to them any different.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Recital

events.title: Eòghann tells the taste cannot be looked for
events.body: Pressed to say what he tasted in the river, Eòghann owns that he cannot put it into words and holds that a man cannot go looking for that taste and find it sooner than he himself found it, kneeling thirsty.

events.body: In his later keeping Eòghann strikes gual teine against flint more than once, hoping the snap of a hand the tellers spoke of might be struck rather than fallen into, and gets from it no more than the ordinary spark any stone gives a blade.

events.body: Eòghann dies in his six-and-sixtieth year at Tobar dhìreach, Poit an Teine burning near him, his last words not of the coals but of the crossing, asking whether the water still ran clear and the light still stood under it.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Recital

events.title: Fewer of the coast-people climb to the temple
events.body: In the years before the temple stands empty for good, those of the landings who still climb to Làrach an Teampaill go up fewer at a time and stay a shorter while at the top, as a household goes on setting a place at table for a while after the one who sat in it has stopped coming.

links.title: Làrach an Teampaill abandoned

told_in.book: Of the Shore, the Sea-Way and the Godkin
told_in.section: I. Of the Empty Sockets

events.title: Làrach an Teampaill abandoned
events.body: The temple is deserted. It is older than any faith that has a name, and its altar looks to the central mountains and the vein beneath them, away from the sea.

events.title: A woman climbs to the temple with empty hands
events.body: A woman of the landings climbs the temple's steps alone at first light and comes down again at evening with nothing in her hands either time, and no one after her is known to climb to Làrach an Teampaill again.

links.title: Làrach an Teampaill abandoned

told_in.book: Of the Shore, the Sea-Way and the Godkin
told_in.section: I. Of the Empty Sockets

events.title: Grass takes the temple platform
events.body: With no foot left to keep it short, the grass between the temple platform's fitted stones grows up thick, and the altar's empty sockets are left to fill and empty again with nothing but whatever season sends into them.

links.label: Legacy

told_in.book: Of the Shore, the Sea-Way and the Godkin
told_in.section: I. Of the Empty Sockets

events.title: Whole kin-groups come down from the abandoned heights
events.body: Where ones and single families once drifted down from the empty heights to settle at the shore, whole kin-groups now come down together, until the landing at Cwen holds more people at once than any landing has held before.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Seann-Dhaoine keep to the shore

told_in.book: Of the Shore, the Sea-Way and the Godkin
told_in.section: II. Of the Middens at Cwen and the Landing-Stones

events.title: A rower teaches the gulls' warning
events.body: Rowers of Slighe-mhara àrsaidh keep a plain word for anyone new to the stretch north of the cape: watch the gulls before you watch the sky, for the birds leave that water before a man in it feels what is coming.

told_in.book: Of the Shore, the Sea-Way and the Godkin
told_in.section: II. Of the Middens at Cwen and the Landing-Stones

events.title: No new work raised out of sight of salt water
events.body: After the high places are left, the people of the landings raise no new work anywhere out of sight of salt water, and the shore takes back all the labour the heights had drawn away.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Seann-Dhaoine keep to the shore

told_in.book: Of the Shore, the Sea-Way and the Godkin
told_in.section: II. Of the Middens at Cwen and the Landing-Stones

events.title: The Seann-Dhaoine keep to the shore
events.body: The high places are left, and every new work of the Seann-Dhaoine is made within sight of salt water. The middens at the southern Seann Chwen begin to grow as fast as those of Seann Dunn once did.

events.title: The midden at Cwen outgrows the midden at Dunn
events.body: The midden below the southern landing at Cwen, thickened season on season by the swelling numbers settled there, grows past the midden at Dunn, which had for a lifetime and more been the largest heap of shell and bone the coast could show.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Seann-Dhaoine keep to the shore

told_in.book: Of the Shore, the Sea-Way and the Godkin
told_in.section: II. Of the Middens at Cwen and the Landing-Stones

events.title: A landing once counted by the dozen is counted by the score
events.body: Two rowers of the sea-way, meeting off a landing-stone, trade the season's news: more households at Cwen than either can remember from a single year before, and a landing further north near empty of the families that once worked it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Seann-Dhaoine keep to the shore

told_in.book: Of the Shore, the Sea-Way and the Godkin
told_in.section: II. Of the Middens at Cwen and the Landing-Stones

events.title: The ancient sea-way
events.body: The boats of the Seann-Dhaoine keep a lane along the south-east coast, from the river mouth below Seann Dunn round the cape where Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg now stands to the bay of Ceann chaol. Flat landing-stones lie along it a day's rowing apart, some grooved still by hauled keels. The Dia-thìrich call it Slighe-mhara àrsaidh, the ancient sea-way, and the fishers of that coast keep to it yet.

links.title: A rower teaches the gulls' warning

links.title: The sea-way's landing-stones grooved by keels

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A father teaches his son the sea-way stone by stone

events.title: The sea-way's landing-stones grooved by keels
events.body: Season on season of hauled keels wear clear grooves into the flat landing-stones of Slighe-mhara àrsaidh along the south-east coast, so that a rower of that lane comes to know each stone by its wear as surely as by its place along the shore.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ancient sea-way

told_in.section: II. Of the Middens at Cwen and the Landing-Stones

events.title: A father teaches his son the sea-way stone by stone
events.body: A rower of Slighe-mhara àrsaidh carries his son in the bow through a whole season's rowing, naming each landing-stone as it comes until the boy's own eye can find the next one before his father's voice does, the same teaching the lane is given, before and after, to every rower's son.

links.title: The ancient sea-way

told_in.section: II. Of the Middens at Cwen and the Landing-Stones

events.title: Rathnait born to the valleys about the crack
events.body: Rathnait is born the third child of a household two ridges east of Tobar dhìreach, of no line that keeps a fire-pot or counts fathers back to the mason by name, but of the valleys about the crack all the same.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Name Said Aloud

events.title: The valleys' dead laid facing the mountains
events.body: The households of the high valleys lay their dead in the ground on their side with the knees drawn up and the face toward the central mountains, with an uncut stone set on end at the head and no mark on it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The hill-folk of the vein

told_in.book: Of the Shore, the Sea-Way and the Godkin
told_in.section: III. Of the Dead Laid in the Ground

events.title: The hill-folk of the vein
events.body: In the high valleys about the crack dwells a people other than the Seann-Dhaoine, who call themselves Clann nan Dè, the godkin. They bury their dead in the ground and not on islands, and they cut no script. Whether they shared the island with the Seann-Dhaoine or came after them, no telling knows; their own word, later, is that they were always there.

events.title: Clann nan Dè settles into ordinary use
events.body: By the time Rathnait is old enough to sit among the elders at her own hearth's turn to hold the gathering, the name Clann nan Dè is said across the valleys about the crack as plainly and as unremarked as any older name tied to a single ridge or ford.

events.title: The first small burning
events.body: At Àth gharbh a sliver of the coloured coal is burnt to a bead in a peat fire by a household not of the Mason's line. It burns black-flamed like any other coal, and the hearthstone round it is stained through with colour. No older burning of the coal by other hands is known. It is a small thing: one sliver, one fire.

events.title: Barabal burns the first sliver outside the line
events.body: At Àth gharbh a woman named Barabal, keeping a bright stone given her as a child at a ford, sets it on her peat fire from idle curiosity; it burns black-flamed like any coal, and the hearthstone beneath it takes a stain of colour clean through its thickness.

events.body: Giorsal is born at Achadh dhìreach, ten miles west of the crack, to a household that keeps no fire-pot and counts no fathers back to the mason, and grows up on Aithris a' Chruthachaidh as every child of the valleys does.

events.title: The stained cloth of Achadh dhìreach
events.body: At Achadh dhìreach the hill-folk rub broken coal from the vein into the wool of the dead, and it takes streaks of a colour no plant dye makes. It is seldom done: one grave in some thirty.

events.body: Giorsal, who sees to the burials of her household, takes up the private habit of rubbing a little broken coloured coal into the wrapping wool of some of her dead, choosing perhaps one grave in thirty across her working years.

events.title: A bright stone is found on the midden at Bral
events.body: A woman of Bral, sifting the midden below her household's huts, turns up a small hard thing bright with more than one colour, unlike any shell or stone the heap has yielded before; no one of that household can say how long it lay there or how it came.

events.body: A chip of the coloured coal, still staining the shell about it, is thrown on a midden at Seann Bhral on the far western coast. By gift, by trade or by theft a piece of the vein came to the Seann-Dhaoine; which, is not known.

events.title: The Children of the Question
events.body: The households of the high valleys begin to call the Mason's line Luchd-ceasnachaidh a' Ghuail Dhìomhair, the Inquisitors of the Mystic Coal, for their long questioning of the two dark coals; the lists shorten it to Clann na Ceiste, the Children of the Question. The kindred take the name, and Clann a' Chlachair is heard less after.

events.title: Lughaidh finds a new-cut stone in the western grass
events.body: Driving his flock further west than his own hearth has grazed before, the shepherd Lughaidh comes on a standing stone raised so lately that the turned earth at its foot has not yet greened over, with no camp, path or tool-litter left by whatever hand set it there.

events.title: Two hands on one stone
events.body: Lughaidh reads a line of unfamiliar script on the stone's upper face, cut broad and level by one hand, and below it four words of his own tongue, Bha teine sa chloich, cut narrower and shallower by another; neither hand has left any other mark on the hillside.

events.body: The tale of the new stone in the western grass passes from Lughaidh's own hearth to the next and on beyond it, the four words kept exact in every mouth that takes them up while the stone's own size and the manner of its finding grow with the telling.

events.title: The words of the low cutting known at every hearth
events.body: By the winter after the western stone is found, every hearth that tells of it tells also what its four low words say, though no one of the valleys reads a sign and no one can say whose mouth first gave the words.

events.body: A woman of Clann na Ceiste sits three days before the western stone to learn which of its two hands came first, and comes home saying both kept their counsel and she will not guess.

events.body: Word of the stone's four words reaches Tobar dhìreach, and the line holds the fire they name for its own, Teine a' Chlachair, while the broader script above them goes on unread, no eye at the line or beyond it able to say what hand cut it or when.

events.title: A second stone found in the stony hills
events.body: A traveller crossing poor, broken ground further into the hills all but walks into a shorter stone before he sees it, and carries down word of three more words cut low upon it, Cuimhnich an teine, in what looks the same sure hand as the first stone's saying.

events.title: The line answers for a bidding cut to no one
events.body: Asked by travellers whether the second stone's plain command speaks to them any clearer than the first, Clann na Ceiste answers each time the same: that the fire is theirs to remember whether the stone bade them or not, there being no other hand on the island that has minded it so long.

events.body: At that year's gathering a young man of the line says Bha teine sa chloich aloud, standing, before the whole crowd for what the tellers hold to be the first time, the saying having come to him by the same slow road as every other hearth, from mouth to mouth, back to a shepherd fifty years gone.

events.body: Mòrnait is born into a household gathered about Clann na Ceiste's own hearth without ever holding its coals, and grows up on Aithris a' Chruthachaidh and the two new sayings both, already part of the ordinary stock of what every child of the valleys knows by then.

events.title: A ring of fire-stones round the pillar
events.body: The ground about Colbh Cnoc chiar is trodden hard in a ring and paved with fire-cracked stones. Fires the size of hearths are kept there again and again. Nothing else is left.

events.title: The ring at the pillar is kept and grows a path
events.body: Mòrnait returns to the ring at Colbh Cnoc chiar year on year, joined in time by others who come to sit an evening by the fire before going their own ways, until a worn path runs to it across the broken ground and the ash within the stones lies black and deep.

events.title: Mòrnait holds the fire is kept, not questioned
events.body: Asked more than once whether her fire is some new trial of the old riddle, Mòrnait answers that the stone asked only to be remembered, not questioned, there being questioning enough already given the two dark coals by better keepers than herself.

events.body: In her sixty-fifth year Mòrnait makes the walk to Colbh Cnoc chiar for the last time, and tells the few who sit with her that evening she does not know what the stone remembers, only that she has kept it as well as she knew how.

events.body: Mòrnait dies at her own hearth some weeks after her last walk, and her daughter, and after her the daughter's own children, take up the walk to the ring in her stead, less often than Mòrnait kept it but often enough that the fire does not go cold.

events.title: Ciannait finds the third stone standing
events.body: Ciannait, driving her household's beasts down to the autumn stubble, finds a squared pillar newly standing on the rise by the drove-road where no stone had stood the year before, and reads aloud, alone but for a boy of her own kin, the four words cut low on its face and the whole saying beneath them.

events.body: Ciannait's brother's boy asks whether the new-found pillar will still be standing come morning; she tells him a stone is not a fire and has never yet been known to go out.

events.body: The hearths that gather to look at the new pillar begin to call the rise Achadh a' Chalbh, a name that settles into use before any household troubles to remember which mouth first gave it.

events.body: At a gathering of some thirty households kept at Achadh a' Chalbh on Oidhche an Dealanaich, an old woman of a neighbouring valley says the sayings of all three stones together before a crowd, and ties the third saying to Aithris a' Chruthachaidh's grass-people and the island as their only root.

events.body: At the first gathering kept at the pillar an old woman of a hearth two valleys east says the sayings of the three stones together for the first time, and says after them that the stone says in fewer words what Aithris a' Chruthachaidh always said.

events.title: The gathering at the column kept a second year, and a third
events.body: More households come to keep the dark of the year at Achadh a' Chalbh than came the winter before, and the ground about the pillar's foot begins to wear bare under their standing, so that within Ciannait's own lifetime the column becomes the one gathering-ground of that whole stretch of country.

events.body: Seathan is born at Tobar dhìreach, the only son of the keeper of gual teine and the rainbow, and has gual teine in his hands from earliest childhood as every child of that hearth has had it before him.

events.title: A market grows up at the column's gatherings
events.body: Traders begin setting hides, salt and wool out on cloths spread over the trampled ground at Achadh a' Chalbh on the two days a year the crowds are greatest, taking their goods up again each evening, for no one yet thinks to leave anything standing there overnight but the stone.

events.body: At Tobar dhìreach a fire-bearer carries the first word of the pillar and its saying to the keeper's own hearth, and a boy not yet six turns gual teine in his fingers as he listens, asking his mother whether the coal and the stone's saying come from the one place.

events.title: The saying carried to the northern shore
events.body: A woman of the northern shore, come south to trade hides for salt at one of Achadh a' Chalbh's market days, hears the whole saying said at the stone and carries it home the length of the island, telling it first at her own hearth to a household that keeps no stone and no gathering-ground of its own.

events.body: A shepherd of the far north-western moor, asked by a passing trader what his own people hold of where they came from, answers with the third stone's four words, though he has never walked south to hear them said at Achadh a' Chalbh himself.

events.body: Seathan's father tells the boy that the bag on its peg has waited longer than any stone in the south, and that a thing worth keeping is worth keeping without asking each year whether the keeping has come to anything.

events.body: On his father's death Seathan takes the bag of two coals and the keeping in his twentieth year, and chooses, unlike his father before him, to keep gual teine near the hearth rather than carry it abroad.

events.body: In the last winter of her life, her joints too cold-bitten for the walk to Achadh a' Chalbh, Ciannait says the third stone's saying once more to her children at her own hearth, tying it plainly to Aithris a' Chruthachaidh of the grass-people grown from the island's own ground.

events.title: Ciannait dies at her own hearth
events.body: Ciannait dies in her one and seventieth year at the hearth where she was born, and is buried, as her own kin have always been buried, without any coal of the vein given her in the ground, that custom never having reached so far south-west in her lifetime.

events.title: Ciannait's children keep the walk to the column after her
events.body: Ciannait's children take up the walk to Achadh a' Chalbh in her stead, not every year but often enough that the fire at the pillar's foot never goes long unlit in their own generation, and the saying she gave them at her hearth goes on being said by mouths that never stood at the stone itself.

events.title: The fire in the fingers
events.body: Seathan of Clann na Ceiste, who has handled the coal of fire all his days to no end, snaps his fingers when a thought strikes him, and the coal-dust on his hand takes fire. He beats it out against his coat and is not burned. So the sixth coal is lit, by the fire that is in the hand itself.

events.body: Word of gual teine's waking spreads beyond the hill country's own hearths, and people begin coming to Achadh a' Chalbh in tens and then in hundreds to hear the recital said at the column, camping about the stone rather than passing it by.

events.body: The shelters at Achadh a' Chalbh are rebuilt so many times over on the footings of the ones before them that a household coming for the first time can see, in the worn hollows and packed earth, that others have stood there before it and will stand there after.

events.body: A burial-ground grows about a place that none remembers hallowing. Its oldest graves are older than the oldest names that can be read there.

events.body: At a great telling at the column a keeper of the bag gives gual bogha-froise into the crowd, and it goes round from hand to hand by firelight through the whole night and comes back to him at dawn as dark as it went out.

events.title: Aoife's child born
events.body: Aoife bears a living child after two she has already lost in their first winters, and lets herself believe, when it survives its own first winter thin but breathing steadily, that this one will live to walk; she sews it, for the first time, a coat cut to its own growing rather than one handed down.

events.body: Aoife, trusting for the first time that a child of hers will live, sews in the last cold months a small coat cut to the child's own growing, a thing she had not let herself do for the two children before.

events.body: A child is buried at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach with a sliver of the coloured coal closed in one hand. The sliver stains still the cloth it is kept in. No other piece of the vein is found with the dead of this age.

events.title: Aoife's child dies
events.body: Aoife's child sickens in the spring and dies quietly in her arms, the third child she has lost and the first she does not hear cry out at the end, so that she says afterward she knew, before she was willing to know it, that this death would not be like the others.

events.body: Aoife's husband's mother says a hearth ought not give a piece of an gual dathach to the dead while the living have use for it, and there are words between the two households that neither afterward cares to keep.

told_in.section: IV. Of Aoife's Child

events.title: The graves begin to keep a line
events.body: The newer graves at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach's western edge begin, without any household deciding it, to be set in a row facing the northern mountains, each new grave drawn to the line the ones before it have already kept, until a household bringing its dead looks for the row before it looks for empty turf.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The rows at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach

told_in.book: Of the Gatherings and the Rows of the Dead
told_in.section: V. Of the Rows That Bent

events.title: A grave dug round an old swelling
events.body: A young man digging his grandfather's grave at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach proposes levelling an old unnamed swelling in his row's path, and is rebuked by an elder digger, who tells him no man may open a grave whose occupant he cannot name; the row bends round it instead.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The rows at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach

told_in.book: Of the Gatherings and the Rows of the Dead
told_in.section: V. Of the Rows That Bent

events.title: An uncle forbids the levelling of an old grave
events.body: A young man digging his grandfather's grave at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach proposes to level an old swelling in the row's path, and his uncle forbids it: a man who cannot say whose grave he opens has no business opening it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The rows at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach

told_in.book: Of the Gatherings and the Rows of the Dead
told_in.section: V. Of the Rows That Bent

events.title: Aoife dies
events.body: Aoife dies in her seventieth year, forty years after burying her child, and is carried to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach and laid in the row nearest the western edge where the child already lies, the row bending as it reaches her grave to keep clear of the old swelling beside it.

links.title: Words between two households over the sliver

told_in.section: V. Of the Rows That Bent

events.title: The rows at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
events.body: The graves at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach begin to be laid in rows, heads toward the central mountains. The first rows are straight. The later ones bend round older graves that no one will disturb.

events.title: The western face of the burial hill woven with bending rows
events.body: Seen from far enough off, the whole western face of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach shows no longer straight lines but a slow curved weaving of rows folding round the swellings no living hand made.

events.title: The panther roads
events.body: The great cats of the island are first seen to keep their roads, crossing the mountains by fixed ways at fixed seasons. Why they do so no one has learned.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Beithir finds the cats' road in the snow

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An old man tells Beithir the cats keep their roads

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Thirty head lost to a broken custom

events.title: Beithir finds the cats' road in the snow
events.body: A herder of the central mountains follows three strayed ewes into a high saddle and finds a line of prints worn into the frozen turf on both sides of it, running straight where the ground gave the beast no cause to turn; his own hearth's elders tell him their fathers knew the same line and the same two turns of year it is kept in.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The panther roads

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: I. Of the Cats That Kept Their Own Time

events.title: An old man tells Beithir the cats keep their roads
events.body: The oldest man of Beithir's hearth tells him that his father and his father's father said the same of that saddle: the great cats of the mountains do not wander the high ground but cross it, at some seasons and not others.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The panther roads

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: I. Of the Cats That Kept Their Own Time

events.title: The crossing season kept
events.body: The hill-folk learn the panthers' seasons and keep off the high passes while the cats cross. The camps in the passes stand empty at the same point in every year.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The gatepost sign first cut

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Àirighean a' Bhealaich stand empty

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The gatepost cut deep enough to read in the scraping

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A boy sent up in error to a stripped shieling

events.title: The gatepost sign first cut
events.body: A household of the high valleys cuts a fresh mark into its gatepost at the turn of year the cats' smell and track return to the passes, and scrapes it away again once both are gone, so that a stranger walking the crossing weeks can read the closed season on every post without asking what the mark means.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The crossing season kept

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: II. Of the Signs on the Gateposts, and the Thirty Head

events.title: Àirighean a' Bhealaich stand empty
events.body: The herders' summer camps on the high passes are found stripped and shuttered at the same point in every year while the cats cross, a boy sent up in error by his father's lost count of days finding one already closed and coming down again with nothing worse than a wasted night's walk.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The crossing season kept

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: II. Of the Signs on the Gateposts, and the Thirty Head

events.title: The gatepost cut deep enough to read in the scraping
events.body: An old woman of the eastern slopes tells a new-married daughter that the crossing mark must be cut deep enough to be read even after it is scraped, so that a late-comer knows the season has been kept there before.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The crossing season kept

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: II. Of the Signs on the Gateposts, and the Thirty Head

events.title: A boy sent up in error to a stripped shieling
events.body: A boy sent up to winter sheep at a shieling in the crossing season, his father having lost the count of days in a wet spell, finds it already stripped and shuttered by households that read the signs, and comes down the same evening.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The crossing season kept

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: II. Of the Signs on the Gateposts, and the Thirty Head

events.title: Thirty head lost to a broken custom
events.body: A herdsman of the lower slopes, trusting his own count of the year over his neighbours' gatepost signs, keeps his cattle ten days past the crossing's start and brings them down to find thirty head missing from the herd, torn on the ground above the track in a way no wolf of that country tears ground.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The panther roads

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: II. Of the Signs on the Gateposts, and the Thirty Head

events.title: The cats turn back at the foothills
events.body: A family watching from a rise above the track sees the crossing cats turn from the eastern passes and go back down toward the western foothills for no cause the watchers can find, and the country reads the plain sign as a warning rather than let it pass unanswered.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The panther roads

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: III. Of the Cats That Turned Back

events.title: The households store double
events.body: On the strength of the turning cats the country stores double against a hard winter that no other sign has yet shown, cutting peat and laying by grain and dried meat past what the ordinary count of mouths at each hearth calls for; the winter that follows proves hard enough to repay the extra carrying.

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: III. Of the Cats That Turned Back

events.title: The hard winter after the cats turned back
events.body: The winter after the cats turn back lays snow to a grown man's waist in the lower valleys for the better part of two months, and every household that stored double says afterward the cutting and the carrying were worth it.

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: III. Of the Cats That Turned Back

events.title: A household scrapes its gatepost early
events.body: A household near the high passes, reading the geese's lateness as a slow season, scrapes its crossing mark bare a full ten days before the cats' smell returns to the saddle above it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eleven lost on the panther road

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: IV. Of Cairbre and the Eleven

events.title: Cairbre and ten set out
events.body: Cairbre leads ten men inland from Teallaichean a' Chladaich, reasoning by the coast's own geese, which have not yet gone over in their numbers that autumn, that the crossing season has not yet begun; a household nearer the mountains has scraped its own gatepost clean on the same late reading and by the same error.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eleven lost on the panther road

links.label: Same person
links.title: The eleven do not come home

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: IV. Of Cairbre and the Eleven

events.title: The eleven do not come home
events.body: Cairbre and the ten who went with him fail to reach the valley they set out for and do not return to the shore; no household along the mountains can say it saw them pass, and winter closes the high ground before any search can be made of it that year.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eleven lost on the panther road

events.title: Eleven lost on the panther road
events.body: A party of eleven from the southern shore goes up into the hills near Cnoc àrsaidh in the crossing season and does not return. Years afterwards their bones are found along the line the cats use still.

events.title: Word comes of a failed harvest inland
events.body: Word reaches Teallaichean a' Chladaich that kin settled two valleys further into the hills than the shore's people commonly go have had their harvest fail badly enough that they will not see the winter through unhelped, and Cairbre resolves to lead ten of his own hearth up to carry it down to them.

told_in.section: IV. Of Cairbre and the Eleven

events.title: Suibhne born at Tobar dhìreach
events.body: A son is born to the household that keeps Poit an Teine and the bag of coals, a big child who closes his hand round a finger held out to him and will not readily let it go, so that they say of him he was born holding on; he is given the name Suibhne.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Suibhne learns the Line standing

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: IV. Of Cairbre and the Eleven

events.title: Cairbre's wife watches the path thirty days
events.body: Cairbre's wife keeps the twelfth day and the fourteenth and the twentieth on the rise above Teallaichean a' Chladaich, and by the thirtieth has stopped telling herself anything, and only watches.

links.title: Eleven lost on the panther road

links.title: Two springs of searching find nothing

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: IV. Of Cairbre and the Eleven

events.title: Two springs of searching find nothing
events.body: The shore and the kin the eleven had set out to help each try the high ground in the spring after they go missing, and again the spring after that, and both times come down with nothing to show for the walking but blistered feet and a country too wide to give up eleven men for the asking.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Cairbre's wife watches the path thirty days

links.label: Same person
links.title: The bones found along the cats' line

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: IV. Of Cairbre and the Eleven

events.title: Suibhne learns the Line standing
events.body: Suibhne, a boy of the keeper's hearth, hears the whole of the Line said over him standing, as every keeper before him had heard it, and learns it.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Suibhne born at Tobar dhìreach

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: IV. Of Cairbre and the Eleven

events.title: The bones found along the cats' line
events.body: A drover's dog worries a length of bone out of the turf off the marked track at the proper close of a crossing season, and searchers over the following days gather a scatter of bone strung along roughly the same course the cats are known to keep, with nothing of what the eleven carried found among it.

links.title: Eleven lost on the panther road

links.title: The eleven buried where they were found

told_in.book: Of the Panther Roads
told_in.section: V. Of the Bones Along the Road

events.title: The eleven buried where they were found
events.body: Unable to say with certainty which bones belonged to which man, the southern shore buries the gathered dead together high on the mountain rather than divide them wrongly among separate graves, and keeps alongside Cairbre's name the plainer lesson the country had already made of the matter: that the crossing months keep a count of their own that no household's calendar has yet learned to keep exactly with it.

links.title: Eleven lost on the panther road

links.title: The bones found along the cats' line

told_in.section: V. Of the Bones Along the Road

events.title: Ailean born to Tobar dhìreach
events.body: A son is born to Suibhne of Clann na Ceiste at Tobar dhìreach, heavier in arm and leg than the women at his birth can readily match against memory, and slow to close his hand on a finger held out to him and slower to let it go, so that his mother says he was born holding on.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Ailean found by Poit an Teine for whole mornings

links.label: Same person
links.title: Suibhne drops the rainbow from Binnean a' Chlachair

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: I. Of a Child Born Slow to Speak

events.title: Ailean found by Poit an Teine for whole mornings
events.body: Ailean, able to sit upright, is found by Poit an Teine for whole mornings together, not reaching for it or troubling it, only sitting near enough to feel its heat and watching the low flame.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Ailean born to Tobar dhìreach

links.label: Same person
links.title: Ailean grows slow of speech and broad of hand

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: I. Of a Child Born Slow to Speak

events.title: Ailean grows slow of speech and broad of hand
events.body: Ailean keeps to single words while children a season younger than him are stringing sentences, and some of his kin wonder aloud whether the line has thrown up a son too plain for the keeping, until his mother points to his hands, already broad at six years old, as proof enough of what manner of man he will be.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Ailean found by Poit an Teine for whole mornings

links.label: Same person
links.title: Ailean's mother answers the talk of his slowness

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: I. Of a Child Born Slow to Speak

events.title: Ailean's mother answers the talk of his slowness
events.body: Ailean's mother puts a stop to the kin's talk of a son too plain for the keeping, saying a slow tongue is no mark against a steady hand, and pointing to his hands.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Ailean grows slow of speech and broad of hand

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: I. Of a Child Born Slow to Speak

events.title: Suibhne drops the rainbow from Binnean a' Chlachair
events.body: In the second year of his keeping Suibhne climbs Binnean a' Chlachair and drops the rainbow from the height of his arm over the same steep side Fearghas used, and it falls to the stones without a flicker.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Ailean born to Tobar dhìreach

links.label: Same person
links.title: Suibhne lays the rainbow beside the burning silver

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: II. Of the Rainbow That Would Not Light

events.title: Suibhne lays the rainbow beside the burning silver
events.body: Suibhne throws the rainbow into the river at the crossing where the silver still burns under the current, so that for a breath the two lie side by side, dark against bright, before the current carries it on.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Suibhne drops the rainbow from Binnean a' Chlachair

links.label: Same person
links.title: Suibhne will not try the rainbow by blood

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: II. Of the Rainbow That Would Not Light

events.title: Suibhne will not try the rainbow by blood
events.body: Suibhne tries the rainbow by the sea, the height, the river and the earth, but will not try it by blood, telling his wife a man ought not open his own hand for a coal that has shown it wants no single element.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Suibhne lays the rainbow beside the burning silver

links.label: Same person
links.title: Suibhne carries the rainbow to Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: II. Of the Rainbow That Would Not Light

events.title: Suibhne carries the rainbow to Doire ghlas
events.body: In his four-and-fortieth year Suibhne walks the three days north to Doire ghlas with gual bogha-froise, the first keeper to bring it to the grove where Coimhdeach na Fine first spoke, and sits under the oaks a night and a day with it held loose in his open hand; it shows him no change of colour or warmth, and he carries it home cold.

links.title: The rainbow coal lit by the Keeper

links.label: Same person
links.title: Suibhne will not try the rainbow by blood

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: II. Of the Rainbow That Would Not Light

events.title: Suibhne says he doubts the rainbow will answer him
events.body: Suibhne tells his own hearth, and not the recital, that he no longer knows whether a man ought to go on asking a question already asked in every way his own life can think to ask it; his son Ailean, sixteen years old, hears it among the last things of any length his father says on the matter.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Suibhne carries the rainbow to Doire ghlas

told_in.section: II. Of the Rainbow That Would Not Light

events.title: Ailean marries Lìobhan
events.body: Ailean, seventeen, takes Lìobhan of a household two valleys west that keeps no coal of its own; she comes to Tobar dhìreach a bride of fifteen and is taught by Suibhne's widow, in the short time left to teach her, how Poit an Teine is fed and the bag kept and what is and is not said of it to a stranger.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Suibhne says he doubts the rainbow will answer him

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: III. Of Lìobhan and the Thought That Came

events.title: Suibhne dies of a fever
events.body: Suibhne dies in his forty-sixth year of a fever that takes him inside a fortnight, with Ailean, eighteen years old and already the broadest man of that hearth, sitting with him through the last nights; the bag of two coals passes to Ailean, though no word of keeping is said over him yet.

links.title: Suibhne says he doubts the rainbow will answer him

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: II. Of the Rainbow That Would Not Light

events.title: Gormshuil born
events.body: A daughter is born to Ailean and Lìobhan in the same wet autumn the household buries Suibhne, and is named Gormshuil for the blue of her eyes at birth, which her grandmother swears she has never seen come on so soon in any other child.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Suibhne dies of a fever

links.label: Same person
links.title: Lìobhan names the rainbow's want

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: III. Of Lìobhan and the Thought That Came

events.title: Lìobhan names the rainbow's want
events.body: Lìobhan says aloud to Ailean what he has half thought and not yet let himself say, that a coal made of every colour together may belong wholly to no single element, as a child of two households belongs wholly to neither; Ailean turns the thought over the whole of that winter until it settles into near certainty.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Gormshuil born

links.label: Same person
links.title: Ailean tells the recital he means to light the six again

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: III. Of Lìobhan and the Thought That Came

events.title: Ailean tells the recital he means to light the six again
events.body: At the recital in his three-and-twentieth year Ailean tells the reciters only that he means, in the year ahead, to light the six coals again by each one's own old way and carry them living to wherever the seventh might at last be answered; the reciters say they will wait to hear how it goes.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Lìobhan names the rainbow's want

links.label: Same person
links.title: Ailean wakes the gold on the northern sea

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: III. Of Lìobhan and the Thought That Came

events.title: Ailean wakes the gold on the northern sea
events.body: Ailean carries a fresh piece of the vein's gold-sheened colour the day's road north to the shore and throws it into the autumn swell as Aodh once did; it takes fire bright gold on the water, and this time he wades in after it and carries it home still burning in a clay pot with a lid of turf.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Ailean tells the recital he means to light the six again

links.label: Same person
links.title: Ailean wakes the snowflake off the height

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: IV. Of the Six Kindled Again

events.title: Ailean wakes the snowflake off the height
events.body: Before winter closes Binnean a' Chlachair, Ailean climbs it in a bitter wind and lets gual sneachda fall from the height of his own arm as Fearghas once let it fall; it catches fire white halfway down the steep side, and he carries both fires down off the summit together.

links.title: Ailean wakes the gold on the northern sea

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: IV. Of the Six Kindled Again

events.title: Ailean wakes the black coal in the earth
events.body: In the last week before the ground freezes hard Ailean digs a grave-deep hole beside the old slab at Tobar dhìreach, lays the black coal in it as Brian once did, and finds it warm and glowing at dawn; three fires now burn under his roof through the shortest days of the year.

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: IV. Of the Six Kindled Again

events.title: Ailean wades after the burning gold
events.body: Where Aodh let the gold burn out on the water, Ailean wades in to the waist after it and catches it still burning between his cupped hands, and carries it home in a clay pot with a turf lid.

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: IV. Of the Six Kindled Again

events.title: Ailean wakes the red-brown coal with his own blood
events.body: In the yard behind his house on a frosted spring morning Ailean sets the red-brown coal on a stone and strikes it as Cormac once struck his; the hammer turns and lays his hand open, and where his blood runs onto the coal a deep warm flame comes up, leaving a scar to match the byname's own.

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: IV. Of the Six Kindled Again

events.title: Ailean wakes the silver in the Abhainn ghorm
events.body: At the crossing below Tobar dhìreach Ailean drinks from his own cupped hands as Eòghann once did and throws gual airgid into the current; it takes fire beneath the running water, and he lifts it out still alight with a wicker scoop made for the purpose.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Ailean wakes the red-brown coal with his own blood

links.label: Same person
links.title: Ailean wakes gual teine on his own doorstone

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: IV. Of the Six Kindled Again

events.title: Ailean wakes gual teine on his own doorstone
events.body: Sitting on his doorstone at midsummer, thinking of nothing to do with fire, Ailean snaps his fingers over dust from the old fire coal without meaning to try anything, as Seathan once did by accident, and the dust flares red-gold and leaves no mark on him; the sixth fire is lit within the same year as the first five.

links.title: Ailean wakes the silver in the Abhainn ghorm

links.title: Ailean sets out north with six fires on a pole

told_in.book: Of Ailean Son of Suibhne
told_in.section: IV. Of the Six Kindled Again

events.title: Ailean sets out north with six fires on a pole
events.body: In the last week of an t-Iuchar Ailean sets out from Tobar dhìreach for Doire ghlas, carrying the six relit coals in clay pots slung from a pole across his shoulders and the dark rainbow coal wrapped against his chest, with Lìobhan and Gormshuil walking beside him as far as the last hearth before the moor.

events.title: Six fires kept under one roof
events.body: Through the last weeks of summer six fires burn in six clay pots under one roof at Tobar dhìreach for the first time since the making of the world, and Ailean wakes at odd hours to see that none has failed.

events.title: Gormshuil watches the lids lifted
events.body: Gormshuil, six years old, kept from the pots by her mother's word, is found more than once crouched at a safe distance watching the lids lifted on the six low fires in their six colours.

events.title: Lìobhan parts from Ailean at the last hearth
events.body: Lìobhan walks with Ailean as far as the last hearth before the moor with Gormshuil on her hip, and tells him only to mind his feet on the wet northern slopes and that she will keep the house fire until he comes home.

events.title: The rainbow coal lit by the Keeper
events.body: Ailean of Clann na Ceiste, having lit each of the six coals again by its own way, carries them burning to the grove at Doire ghlas with the last coal, which his kindred have tried for more than four hundred years. The Keeper comes to him there and lights the rainbow coal, and for the first time all seven burn together, each from its own spirit. It bids him stay with them until they are cold.
